en: Arjuna said:
O mighty-armed one, I desire to know the true nature of renunciation.
And [tell me] of renunciation, O Hṛṣīkeśa, separately, O slayer of Keśin. //1//
Śrīdhara:

In the eighteenth chapter, for the sake of determining the supreme truth, he clearly stated the summary of the entire meaning of the Gītā through the distinction between ritual assignment (*nyāsa*) and renunciation (*tyāga*).
And in this regard:
"Having renounced all actions with the mind, the self-controlled one dwells in happiness" (Gītā 5.13).
In passages such as "one whose self is disciplined by the yoga of renunciation" (Gītā 9.28), the renunciation of action is taught; likewise: "having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action..."
Ever contented and dependent on nothing,
then, with self-restraint, practice the renunciation of the fruits of all actions. (Gītā 4.20)
In such passages as these, the performance of action is taught through the renunciation of the fruit alone;
and the Lord, who is omniscient and supremely compassionate, would not teach things that are mutually contradictory.
Therefore, desiring to understand the manner in which the renunciation of action and its performance are not in conflict, Arjuna said: "Of renunciation... and so forth.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, controller of all the senses!

O slayer of Keśin! When the great Daitya named Keśin, who had assumed the form of a horse, came with his mouth wide open to devour you in battle, you thrust your left arm into that exceedingly gaping maw; and at that very moment, by means of that very [arm] having expanded, [you tore him asunder].
Having torn him open with his arm like a *karkaṭikā* fruit, he killed him;
therefore, he is addressed as "O Mahābāho" (O mighty-armed one).
I wish to know the truth of *sannyāsa* (renunciation) and *tyāga* (abandonment) separately, through discernment. //1//
Viśvanātha:
The threefold nature of renunciation, knowledge, and action; the determination of liberation; and devotion as the most secret essence—these are said to be the eighteen [chapters].
In the immediately following chapter:
"Therefore, performing acts of sacrifice and austerity without aiming for their fruit..."

In this statement of the Blessed One, "And various acts of giving are performed by those desiring liberation" (Gītā 17.25), the term "those desiring liberation" refers specifically to renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*).
Or if they are indeed different from others,

then what is that renunciation of those renouncers of the fruits of all actions whom you have described in the verse: "Therefore, with self-control, practice the renunciation of the fruits of all actions" (Gītā 12.11)?
And one who desires to know through discrimination what that renunciation (*sannyāsa*) of the renunciants (*sannyāsins*) is, asks: "Of renunciation...
[The word *pṛthak* (separately) means: if the two words "renunciation" and "abandonment" have distinct meanings, then I wish to know the true nature of renunciation and abandonment separately;
but if they have the same meaning—whether in your own doctrine or in another's doctrine—then I wish to know their identity of meaning, that is, their oneness of purpose, separately.

The sense is: because You, O Hṛṣīkeśa, are the prompter of my intellect, You alone cause this doubt to emerge; and because You, O Keśinisūdana, are the one who tears asunder that very doubt just as Keśin was torn apart, You alone are the one who destroys it.

Furthermore, O Mahābāho, while You are endowed with the strength of great arms and I am endowed with only a little strength of arms, Your friendship with me is based on this single factor alone, and not otherwise.
The meaning is that, because of the partial friendship granted by You through qualities such as omniscience, I am free from hesitation in answering this question. //1//
Baladeva:
Summarizing here all the meanings of the Gītā in this eighteenth chapter, Hari spoke of the extreme secrecy of both devotion and surrender therein.

"Having renounced all actions with the mind, the self-controlled one dwells happily" (Gītā 5.13). Regarding such passages, Arjuna, being in doubt as to what was meant by the word *sannyāsa* here, and what was meant by the word *tyāga* in passages such as "having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action" (Gītā 4.20), asks: "Of renunciation... [and so forth].
Are the words *sannyāsa* and *tyāga* of different meanings, like the words "mountain" and "tree," or are they of similar meaning, like the words "Kuru" and "Pāṇḍava"?
If it is the former, then I wish to know the true nature of renunciation (*sannyāsa*) and abandonment (*tyāga*) separately.
If it is the latter, then there will be only a distinction based on internal limiting conditions (*upādhi*).
And I wish to know that.
O mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa—because you are the impeller of the functions of the intellect, you alone cause this doubt to arise in me.
O slayer of Keśin, destroy my doubt as you did the demon Keśin. //1//
The Blessed Lord said:
The wise know that the renunciation of actions performed for the sake of desire is *saṃnyāsa*.
The wise declare that renunciation is the relinquishing of the fruits of all actions. //2//
Śrīdhara: To that, the Blessed Lord gave this reply: "Of the optional rites" (*kāmyānām*).

The wise know *nyāsa*—that is, renunciation or *saṃnyāsa*—to be the abandonment of those actions prescribed with a connection to specific desires, such as "one desiring a son should sacrifice," "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," and so forth.
The meaning is that the learned understand *nyāsa*, or *saṃnyāsa*, to be the relinquishing of even all actions together with their proper fruits.

The wise and discerning declare that "renunciation" consists solely in the renunciation of the fruits of all actions—whether those performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), or those that are obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*). They do not mean the renunciation of the action itself in its essential form. Now, one might object: since no fruit is mentioned for obligatory and occasional rites, how can there be a renunciation of a fruit that does not exist?
For the abandonment of a son by a barren woman is not possible.

It is said: although no specific fruit is heard of in such injunctions as "one desiring heaven," "one desiring cattle," and so forth, or in "one should perform the twilight worship daily" and "one should offer the Agnihotra as long as one lives," nevertheless, a discerning person would not engage in an activity that does not serve a human purpose.

Being unable to impel [the agent] to act, an injunction necessarily implies some result in a general sense, as in cases such as "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit. Nor should it be thought that the purpose of the injunction is merely its own establishment through faith, for that would not be a sufficiently weighty motive; otherwise, the impossibility of human engagement [with the rite] would be difficult to avoid.

And a fruit is indeed heard even in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and others: "All these become possessors of meritorious worlds," "By action one attains the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*"),
and "By dharma they dispel evil," and so forth.
Therefore, it is rightly said: "The wise declare that renunciation is the relinquishing of the fruits of all actions.
Now, one might object: "But by relinquishing the fruit, would there not be no engagement at all in actions that are otherwise fruitless?
This is not so, because all actions are enjoined for the purpose of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), through their distinct application (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktva*).
And thus says the Śruti: "The Brāhmaṇas seek to know Him through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting.
Therefore, having abandoned all fruits mentioned in the words of the Śruti as being binding, the performance of all actions for the sake of the desire to know (vividiṣā) is indeed appropriate.

And this desire to know consists in the inward inclination of the intellect, resulting from the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal realities and the cessation of identification with the body and so forth.

Furthermore, for one who performs necessary actions as appropriate and not contrary to knowledge for the sake of purifying the being up to that limit, the very renunciation of the fruit of those actions is what is called "renunciation of action," not its renunciation in its own nature.
And thus says the Śruti: "Performing actions here alone, one should desire to live a hundred years" (Īśa Upaniṣad 2).
But thereafter, the cessation of all ritual action occurs spontaneously.
As it is said in the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*:
"Having produced an inclination of the intellect toward the inner Self through purification by means of rituals..."
Having accomplished their purpose, they set like clouds at the end of the rainy season.
And it was said by the Blessed One: "But he who should find delight only in the self," and so forth.
And it was said by Vasiṣṭha: "The yogin should not abandon his actions."
"For it is abandoned by means of actions,
through the very destruction of *saṅkalpa*, which is the root of action. Thus [it is said].
Or, perceiving that it causes distraction from steadfastness in knowledge, one should abandon it;
as it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam:
"One should perform ritual actions only so long [as they do not distract from knowledge]."
One should not become weary until such time as faith arises toward listening to my teachings and other such practices. (BhP 11.20.9)
Whether established in knowledge, or dispassionate,
or a devotee of Me, being free from expectations,
one should abandon the stages of life along with their external marks.
"One should act outside the scope of prescribed rules," and so forth.
Enough with this digression; let us return to the subject at hand. //2//

Viśvanātha: First, relying on the Eastern (Prācya) school of thought, he states that the words *sannyāsa* and *tyāga* have distinct meanings, beginning with the verse "kāmyānām. The sense is this: they know *sannyāsa*—which is abandonment (*nyāsa*) by way of renunciation (*tyāga*)—to apply only to those "optional" (*kāmya*) rites enjoined with a specific desire, such as "one desiring a son should sacrifice" or "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," and not even to the obligatory (*nitya*) rites such as the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*).

The fruits of all optional rites as well as obligatory rites are indeed established by such scriptural passages as, "Through action, the world of the ancestors [is attained]," and "One dispels evil through dharma. Therefore, renunciation (*tyāga*) consists in performing all actions while being devoid of any desire for their fruits;
whereas renunciation in the sense of *saṃnyāsa* consists in performing only the obligatory rites while being devoid of any desire for their fruits.

However, it should be understood that the distinction [between these two types of renunciation] is that, in the case of optional rites (*kāmya-karman*), renunciation occurs by their very nature. //2//
Baladeva: Being thus questioned, the Blessed One said, "Of those performed for desire.

The meaning is that the wise—the learned—know *sannyāsa* to be the renunciation, that is, the abandonment in its own form, of those rites such as the *putreṣṭi* sacrifice and the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice which are enjoined through the connection with specific desires, such as "one desiring a son should sacrifice" or "one desiring heaven should sacrifice"; but not of the obligatory rites such as the *agnihotra*.

Among these, the wise declare that the characteristic renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is indeed the relinquishment of the fruits of all actions—both those performed out of desire and those that are obligatory—but not their relinquishment in terms of their essential nature.
Furthermore, obligatory actions do have a fruit, for it is heard in scripture: "By action one attains the world of the ancestors; by dharma one removes evil," and so forth.

Although no specific fruit is heard in such injunctions as "one should perform the twilight worship daily" or "one should offer the Agnihotra as long as one lives"— unlike [injunctions] such as "one desiring a son should sacrifice"— nevertheless, like the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," the mandate must necessarily imply some fruit.
Otherwise, since human activity would be untenable, an unavoidable difficulty would arise;
and thus, there would be an abandonment of optional rites (*kāmya-karman*) in their own nature.

However, the meaning of the word *sannyāsa* (renunciation) with respect to obligatory duties (*nitya-karmans*) is the relinquishment of their fruit. Indeed, the meaning of the word *tyāga* (relinquishment) is the performance of all actions after having abandoned the desire for their results.
By the reasoning stated previously, the objection that non-engagement is unavoidable because the fruit of the arising of knowledge exists, has been refuted. //2//
"Action should be abandoned as being full of evil," so some wise men have said;
others, however, say that the action consisting of sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity should not be abandoned. (18.3)
Śrīdhara: For the ignorant person, the meaning of the word "renunciation" (tyāga) is merely the renunciation of the fruit;
it is not the renunciation of the action itself.
He shows this very distinction between opinions in order to strengthen his position by refuting other views, beginning with the words "that which is to be abandoned."
"Indeed, because [action] such as violence is faulty—that is, because it is a cause of bondage—it follows that all action must be abandoned; thus some wise Sāṅkhyas have declared.
This is the meaning: the prohibition "one should not harm any living beings" states that for a person, violence is a cause of misfortune;
however, a scriptural injunction within a specific context, such as "one should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma," states that violence serves to assist the ritual (*kratu*).

Therefore, because their objects are distinct, they do not fall within the scope of the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-nyāya*), and thus there is no relationship of sublation (*bādhya-bādhakatā*).

Furthermore, since injury (*hiṃsā*) and the like are possible in all ritual actions (*karman*) that have material substances as their means of accomplishment (*dravya-sādhya*), every such action must indeed be abandoned.
As it has been said: "For the scriptural (*ānuśravika*) [means] is like the perceptible (*dṛṣṭavat*); it is characterized by impurity, decay, and excess."
The meaning of this is as follows: that which is heard in succession from the recitation of a teacher is *anuśrava*, which is the Veda.
The means of attainment, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, which is taught by that [Veda], is *ānuśravika*.
In that regard, impurity is indeed violence;
likewise, decay is destruction.
Furthermore, there exists a gradation among the heavens produced by such rites as the Agnihotra and the Jyotiṣṭoma.
But the excellence of others causes everyone to suffer.

However, other Mīmāṃsakas say that rituals such as sacrifices must not be abandoned. The point is this: although this violence is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), it must nevertheless be performed by the person.
And even when performed with another person as the intended object, that [act] remains a cause of transgression for the man;
for just as an injunction prescribes the performance of what is to be enjoined with that [intended object] as its purpose,
since being a subordinate element (śeṣatva) is characterized by being for the sake of that [primary object].
However, a prohibition does not require that purpose [of the primary injunction] for its own negation, because it requires only the prior occurrence [of the action].
Otherwise, there would follow the absurdity of the absence of fault even in cases committed through ignorance, negligence, and so forth.
Thus, since the general rule is sublated by the specific one due to their having the same object, there is no presence of fault.
Therefore, sacrificial and other such rites must never be abandoned.
By this, the equal force of injunctions and prohibitions is set aside in order to establish the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-nyāya*). //3//
Viśvanātha: Regarding renunciation, he again introduces a difference of opinion with the words "it is to be abandoned.
Some, namely the Sāṅkhyas, hold that action is to be abandoned even in its very nature because it possesses defects such as violence (*hiṃsā*).
Others, the Mīmāṃsakas, say that actions such as sacrifice are not to be abandoned because they are enjoined by the scriptures. //3//
Baladeva: Regarding renunciation, he again states the difference of opinion with the words "it is to be abandoned.

Some wise men—the followers of Kapila (Kāpilas)—who point to the Vedic injunction "one should not harm any living beings" as being defective, say that [action] is to be abandoned because it is possessed of defects such as the injury to animals; thus, it is to be rejected by its very nature.

The scriptural injunction, "One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma," indeed declares that violence is an auxiliary element of the ritual; however, it does not preclude its status as a cause of harm.
Thus, since violence is possible through the use of material substances, [the opponent argues that] every action should be abandoned.

Other followers of Jaimini, however, say that sacrificial acts and the like are not to be abandoned because they are faultless due to being ordained by the Veda; for even though such action consists of injury and favor, nevertheless, because its status as dharma is declared by the Veda, it possesses no fault, and therefore it must indeed be performed— this is the meaning.
The general prohibition "one should not kill," however, declares that act to be sinful in cases other than a sacrifice; thus, there is nothing objectionable here. //3//
Listen to my definitive conclusion regarding renunciation, O best of the Bharatas. For renunciation, O tiger among men, is declared to be of three kinds. (18.4)
Śrīdhara: Having thus presented the difference of opinions, he says "Listen to the certainty" in order to state his own view.
Regarding that very renunciation about which there is such disagreement, listen to the certainty from my words.
Do not disregard this by thinking, "Since renunciation is well-known in the world, what is there here to be heard?"—thus he says, "O tiger among men," meaning O best of men.
This renunciation is difficult to understand;
for this renunciation of action is proclaimed by those who know reality through correct discernment as being threefold, according to the divisions of tamasic and so forth.
And he will explain this threefold nature starting with the words, "But renunciation of obligatory action... (Gītā 18.7).
Viśvanātha: He states his own view with the words "niścayam" (the certainty).
It is threefold: *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*.
Having thus described the threefold nature of renunciation (*tyāga*), [he says]: "But the renunciation of obligatory action is not possible."
The abandonment of that [action] out of delusion is proclaimed to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).

Thus, because the word *sannyāsa* is applied to that very [renunciation] through its various tamasic divisions, it is understood that in the opinion of the Blessed One, the words *tyāga* and *sannyāsa* have precisely the same meaning. //4//
Baladeva: Having thus described the difference of opinions, he states his own view with the words "the certainty.
Listen to my certainty regarding renunciation for the sake of the Supreme Lord, the omniscient one, since [renunciation] has been seized by conflicting views.
Now, one might object: since renunciation is already well-known, what is there to be heard regarding it?

Regarding this, he says: "For renunciation... Since renunciation is proclaimed—that is, explained in detail—by the wise as being threefold according to the divisions of *tāmasa* and so forth, it is difficult to understand; therefore, its threefold nature must be heard.
However, that which begins with "But for one who is fixed" (niyatasya tu) shall be stated later [in verse 4].
The action consisting of sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity is not to be abandoned; it must indeed be performed.
For sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity are the purifiers of the wise. (18.5)

Śrīdhara: First, he states his firm conclusion with two verses beginning with "yajña. These are purifying for the wise—that is, for those possessed of discernment—meaning they bring about the purification of the mind. (5)

Viśvanātha: Among even those actions performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), the Lord’s view is that sacrifices, gifts, and austerities of a *sāttvika* nature should be performed by those free from longing for fruits; thus He says, "Sacrifices and so forth must indeed be performed.
The reason for this is stated as "because they are purifying" (*pāvanāni*), which means because they effect the purification of the mind. //5//
Baladeva: First, he states his own conviction regarding that matter in two verses beginning with "yajña.

Sacrifices and other such acts are indeed duties for the wise and are not to be abandoned; for these, like a thread of poison, become purifiers through the medium of knowledge that has arisen within, and they serve to destroy the defects of worldly existence. //5//
"But even these actions, O Pārtha, must be performed after abandoning attachment and the fruits; this is my settled and supreme opinion. (18.6)
Śrīdhara: Showing the manner in which these [actions] become purifying when performed, he says, "These...
Those actions such as sacrifice and so forth which I have described as purifying must indeed be performed in this way.
How? Having abandoned attachment—that is, the insistence on being the agent—they must be performed solely as worship of the Lord.
It is my firm conviction that actions must be performed even after renouncing their fruits;
for this very reason, it is the highest [path]. //6//

Viśvanātha: He shows the manner in which these [actions], when performed, become purifying, with the words "even these. "Attachment" (*saṅgam*) means the insistence on agency (*kartṛtvābhiniveśa*) and the expectation of fruit (*phalābhisandhim*).
The sense is that the very abandonment of both the expectation of fruit and the insistence on agency is what is called "abandonment" (*tyāga*) and "renunciation" (*sannyāsa*). //6//
Baladeva: He states the manner in which sacrifices and other rites are purifying by saying, "Even these.

Having abandoned attachment—which is the insistence on agency—as well as the fruits and all the worlds of the ancestors and so forth mentioned previously, these acts must be performed with the sole intention of worshipping the Lord; this is my firm conviction.
Therefore, this is the highest doctrine.
Because it also includes the relinquishing of the attachment to agency, the doctrine of Pārthasārathi is superior. //6//
But the renunciation of prescribed action is not appropriate; its abandonment through delusion is proclaimed to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). (18.7)
Śrīdhara: Having thus declared the threefold nature of renunciation, he now demonstrates it through the three verses beginning with "niyatasya.
Since optional (kāmya) action is binding, its renunciation is appropriate;
however, the renunciation—that is, the abandonment—of obligatory (niyata), that is, daily (nitya), action is not tenable.

Because it is a cause of liberation by means of purifying the *sattva*, its abandonment—even though it is something to be adopted—would arise solely from delusion (*moha*), characterized as such; and since that delusion is of the nature of *tamas*, it is proclaimed to be *tāmasa*. //7//
Viśvanātha: He describes the *tāmasa* variety of the threefold renunciation under discussion: "of that which is fixed" (niyatasya), meaning obligatory;
"out of delusion" (mohāt), meaning from ignorance of the intent of the scriptures (*śāstra*).
Let the renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) indeed renounce optional rites (*kāmya-karman*), since there is no necessity for them; however—
The meaning of the word "tu" (but) is that the abandonment of obligatory duty (*nitya-karman*) is not tenable.
"Out of delusion" means out of ignorance;
"tamasic" indicates that the fruit of tamasic abandonment is precisely the attainment of ignorance.
But the sense is that there is no attainment of the desired knowledge. //7//
Baladeva: With the three verses beginning with "niyatasya," He declares the threefold nature of renunciation previously promised.
Since optional (kāmya) action is binding, its renunciation is appropriate;
however, the renunciation—that is, the abandonment—of obligatory (niyata), constant, and occasional action, such as the great sacrifices (mahāyajña), is not tenable.

Because that [body] contains internal knowledge—which, like a shattered vessel and so forth, is the liberator—and because it effects the maintenance of the body's journey, its abandonment is not proper.

For by means of that [body], the majesty of the Lord as deity is worshipped; by the pure remnants of that worship, the maintenance of the body's journey is accomplished for the sake of attaining knowledge of reality (tattva-jñāna).
In the opposite case, that which was previously stated—"Perform your obligatory duty" (Gītā 3.19) and so forth—applies even to that [abandonment].
Abandonment by way of its own nature, due to delusion—that is, from ignorance that "this is a bond"—is tamasic, because delusion is a property of darkness (tamas). //7//

If one should abandon action merely because it is painful, out of fear of physical hardship, he performs a renunciation that is passionate (rājasa) and shall not obtain the fruit of renunciation. (18.8)
Śrīdhara: He describes the *rājasa* renunciation with the words "It is painful" (*duḥkham*).

That which is the act of an agent who, lacking self-knowledge, renounces obligatory duty merely out of fear of physical exertion, thinking "it is simply pain"—such a renunciation is *rājasa*, because the pain is of a *rājasa* nature.

Therefore, having performed that *rājasa* renunciation, that *rājasa* person does not at all obtain the fruit of renunciation, which is characterized by steadfastness in knowledge; this is the meaning. //8//
Viśvanātha: "It is simply suffering" means:

although I certainly know that for obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) their performance is indeed necessary and that there is only merit in doing them, not fault, nevertheless, the intention is: "How can I let this body be needlessly tormented by those [rites]?"
One would not obtain knowledge, which has renunciation as its fruit. //8//

Baladeva: Even one who desires liberation might abandon prescribed action—though knowing it to be the cause of liberation when performed without desire—out of fear of bodily affliction, thinking that such acts as the acquisition of wealth and morning ablutions are of the nature of suffering. That abandonment is *rājasa*, because suffering is a quality of *rajas*.
Even after making that renunciation, a person would not obtain its fruit, which is steadfastness in knowledge. //8//

O Arjuna, when obligatory action is performed simply because it ought to be done, having abandoned attachment as well as the fruit, that renunciation is considered to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika). 18.9.
Śrīdhara: He describes the *sāttvika* renunciation with the words "kāryam" and so forth.

That renunciation is considered *sāttvika* wherein action is performed—having abandoned attachment and fruit—after it has been determined as "kāryam," meaning it is prescribed as something that must necessarily be done. //9//
Viśvanātha: "Nitya" (constant) action is that which is performed with the conviction that it must necessarily be done;
"sāttvika" means that through such renunciation, he shall surely obtain the fruit of renunciation, which is knowledge—this is the intended meaning. //9//

Baladeva: That which is performed by abandoning attachment, the insistence on agency, and the fruit entirely—so that the action (*kārya*), being prescribed as something necessarily to be done, becomes "regulated" (*niyata*)—that is Sāttvika renunciation, because such knowledge is a quality of *sattva*. //9//
The renouncer, pervaded by purity, wise and with doubts severed, does not hate unwholesome action nor does he cling to wholesome action. (18.10)
Śrīdhara: He states the characteristics of one who is firmly established in such Sāttvika renunciation in the passage beginning with "he does not hate" (*na dveṣṭi*).
One who is "pervaded by Sattva" (*sattva-samāviṣṭaḥ*), meaning completely permeated by Sattva, is a Sāttvika renouncer.
He does not hate unwholesome action—that is, action that brings about suffering, such as the morning bath during the winter season.
Furthermore, he does not become attached to—that is, he does not take pleasure in—wholesome actions that produce immediate happiness, such as bathing at midday during the summer heat.
The reason for this is that he is wise and of steady intellect;

since he endures even great suffering such as humiliation from others and renounces pleasures such as those of heaven, how insignificant is this momentary happiness and suffering compared to that? Thus he reflects.
This is the meaning.
For this very reason, he is one whose doubt and false knowledge have been severed, and who is characterized by neither the desire to acquire nor the desire to avoid bodily pleasure and pain. //10//
Viśvanātha: He states the characteristic of one who is firmly established in such sattvic renunciation in the verse beginning with "na dveṣṭi" (he does not hate), and so forth.
He does not hate what is unwholesome—that is, unpleasant—such as morning baths in the cold; nor does he crave what is wholesome—that is, pleasant—such as bathing in the heat of summer. //10//
Baladeva: He states the characteristics of one who renounces with *sattva* in the verse beginning with "he hates not.

He does not hate what is unwholesome—that which causes suffering, such as bathing in the early morning during the winter—and he does not become attached to what is wholesome—that which bestows pleasure, such as bathing at midday during the summer.

For he is one who, being possessed of goodness (sattva), is exceedingly self-controlled, wise, and firm-minded, yet has cut through the doubt characterized by the question: "Will these performed actions, though executed with effort, produce knowledge or not?"—he is such a person.
Such a person is to be understood as one who renounces with sattvic motivation. //10//
Indeed, it is not possible for one who bears a body to renounce actions entirely;
however, he who renounces the fruits of action is called a "renouncer. (18.11)

Śrīdhara: [Objection: Surely, the renunciation of all actions is better than such a renunciation of the fruits of action; for that being the case, the steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*) is easily attained due to the absence of distraction caused by action. To this, he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*).
For one who bears a body—that is, one who possesses the conceit of identifying the body with the self—it is not possible to renounce all actions completely.
This has been stated [in the Gītā]: "Indeed, no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action," and so forth.
Therefore, he who, even while performing actions, is a renouncer of the fruits of action—he alone is called a happy renouncer (mukha-tyāgī). //11//
Viśvanātha: For this reason as well, he says "na hi" (not indeed) to show that scriptural action must not be abandoned.
It is not possible to abandon them; they cannot be avoided.
As it has been said: "Indeed, no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action. (11)

Baladeva: If it be argued that the renunciation of action in its very nature is superior to such renunciation of its fruits—because, by the absence of distraction, it serves as a means for steadfastness in knowledge—the Lord says "no" (na hi) in response.
For one who bears a body, actions cannot be renounced entirely; they are not possible to renounce. As it has been said: "Indeed, no one even for a moment," and so forth.
Therefore, he who performs actions while indeed renouncing their fruits is alone called a "renouncer.

Thus, it is the opinion of Pārtha’s charioteer that a qualified aspirant, being free from attachment to agency and desire for results, should perform all actions according to his capacity for the sake of knowledge. //11//
The threefold fruit of action— undesirable, desirable, and mixed— accrues after death to those who do not renounce, but never to those who have truly renounced. (18.12)

Śrīdhara: He states the fruit of such renunciation of the fruits of action in the words "the undesired," etc. The undesired is the state of being a hell-being; the desired is the state of being a deity.
The mixed state is that of humanity.
Thus, whatever fruit is well-known to result from the threefold action— whether sinful, meritorious, or both mixed—
is all experienced after death in the hereafter only by those who do not renounce and who possess desires.
This occurs because those [others] possess the threefold nature of action,
whereas it never occurs for renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*).
Here, by the word "renunciant," even those who have renounced the fruits of action under discussion are included, due to their similarity in the renunciation of results.

The meaning is as follows: since the term "renunciant" (saṃnyāsin) is seen to be applied to those who have renounced the fruits of action in such passages as, "He who performs the necessary work without depending on the fruit of action is both a renunciant and a yogi," there can be no sin for those sattvic persons; and because they have renounced the fruit of merit by offering it to the Lord, the threefold fruit of action does not accrue to them. //12//
Viśvanātha: He states the fault that arises in the absence of such renunciation: "The undesirable (is) the suffering of hell; the desirable (is) the happiness of heaven;
and the mixed (is) the pleasure and pain in human birth—these belong only to non-renouncers, that is, to those devoid of such renunciation, after death in the next world. //12//
Baladeva: He states the fault that arises from the absence of such renunciation with the words "the undesirable" (*aniṣṭam*).
The undesirable is the state of being a denizen of hell;
the desirable is the state of being in heaven; and the mixed is the state of being human.
The fruit of action is threefold, consisting of the experience of pain, pleasure, and their combination;
it occurs after death, in a future time, for those who do not renounce— that is, for those devoid of the aforementioned renunciation—
but not for renunciants who possess that aforementioned renunciation.
However, for them, liberation occurs through knowledge that is internalized within their actions; thus, the fruit of renunciation has been described. //12//
O mighty-armed one, learn from me these five causes declared in the Sāṃkhya system of definitive conclusion for the successful accomplishment of all actions. (18.13)

Śrīdhara: Now, having raised the doubt—"How can there be no fruit of action for one who performs action?"—he says these five verses beginning with "pañca" (five) in order to establish that there is no taint by the fruit of action for one who has abandoned attachment and is free from egoism. For the accomplishment—that is, the completion—of all actions, learn from my words these five causes that are about to be described.

"These must necessarily be known for the purpose of removing the conceit of agency in the self"— it is with this in mind that he speaks of "Sāṅkhya" for the sake of praising them. Sāṅkhya is the knowledge of reality, so called because by means of it the Supreme Self (paramātman) is correctly (samyak) enumerated (khyāyate) or known.
The self-knowledge that is manifest is Sāṅkhya.
Because action performed within it finds its end or completion therein, it is called Sāṅkhya.
Furthermore, because the final determination (anta) has been made (kṛta) in this [treatise], the Sāṅkhya scripture itself is called Kṛtānta.
"In that [work] they have been declared;
therefore, understand them correctly"—this is the meaning.

Viśvanātha: Now, raising the objection, "But how can there be no fruit of action for one who performs action?", he says, beginning with "The five," in order to demonstrate that when there is absence of egoism (*nirahaṅkāratva*), there is no taint of action (*karma-lepa*).
Through five [causes]. For the accomplishment and completion of all actions, learn—understand—from my words these five causes.
Regarding the Sāṅkhya: that which correctly explains (khyāti) the Supreme Self is "saṅkhya"; thus, it is Sāṅkhya, namely the Vedānta scripture. In that [Sāṅkhya], [these five causes are taught].
"In what kind [of state] is the action performed such that its end—its destruction—is found therein? These have been declared.

Baladeva: If it is asked, "Why would those who perform actions not experience their fruits?", the intention is that this occurs by abandoning the insistence on one's own agency and by ascertaining the Supreme Lord as the primary agent; with this in mind, he says "these five" in the following five verses.
O mighty-armed one, for the sake of the accomplishment—that is, the completion—of all actions, learn from me these five causes; know them.
He states their authority: "In the Sāṅkhya.
Sāṅkhya is knowledge; the Vedānta scripture which expounds that [knowledge] is Sāṅkhya; [it is] in that [scripture].

To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says: it is that which effects the determination in the *kṛtānta*—that is, the final conclusion—that the Supreme Self is the instigator of all causes consisting of karma; this is the meaning.
This is known to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) Brahman.
Here too [it is said]: "And I am in the heart of all" (Gītā 15.15).
Thus it has been said, and it will also be said: "The Lord is the master of all beings" (Gītā 18.61), and so forth.
The locus, as well as the agent, the various kinds of instruments, the diverse and distinct activities, and destiny as the fifth— these constitute action here. (18.14)
Śrīdhara says: He states those very things as "the locus" (adhiṣṭhāna) and so forth. The locus is the body;
the agent is the ego (ahaṅkāra), which is a knot of the conscious and the unconscious.
"Of various kinds" means of many types;
"instrument" refers to the eye, ear, and so forth;
they are diverse both in terms of their function and their essential nature.
The distinct activities of the vital breaths, such as inhalation (prāṇa) and exhalation (apāna), are their functions.
In this context, this very fifth cause is destiny (daiva);
it is either the internal ruler (antaryāmī) who impels all things, such as the sun, which assist the eyes and other faculties, or [the unseen force]. //14//
Viśvanātha: He enumerates those very [factors]:
study (adhitih), the substratum (adhiṣṭhānam) which is the body, and the agent (kartā), which is the ego-sense (ahaṅkāraḥ)—the knot of the conscious and the unconscious.
The instruments are the eye, ear, and so forth;
they are of various kinds, meaning of many types.
Their distinct activities are the separate functions of the out-breath, in-breath, and so on.
The divine is the impeller of all and the inner controller. //14//

Baladeva: He enumerates those very [causes]: "study," etc. That which is presided over by the individual soul (*jīva*) is the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*), namely the body; the agent is the individual soul. Scripture declares its status as knower and agent through such passages as, "For he is the seer, the creator" (*Praśna Upaniṣad* 4.9).
And the author of the Sūtras states: "It is a knower for this very reason" (*Brahma Sūtra* 2.3.18).
And there are [sūtras] such as "Thus, the agent [is established], because the scripture would otherwise be purposeless" (VS 3.2.26).
The instrument (*karaṇa*) consists of the ear and other senses together with the mind;
it is of various kinds, performing distinct functions for the accomplishment of various actions.

And "various distinct activities" refers to the manifold, separate functions of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the downward breaths (apāna), and so forth. Regarding the term "fate" (daiva): here, within the collection of causes that brings about the completion of action, fate is the supreme Brahman, the one to be propitiated by all, as the fifth factor.
The meaning is that Lord Hari, acting as the inner controller (antaryāmī), is the primary cause in the accomplishment of action.

The meaning is this: for those who possess the certainty that the soul has the body, senses, vital breaths, and the individual self as its instruments and is the instigator of action, their actions do not lead to bondage—provided they are devoid of the attachment to agency and the longing for the fruits of those actions.
Now, one might object: if the soul's agency depends upon the Supreme Lord, then it follows that the soul would be subject to the Lord's own command.
Because [the person] would be equivalent to a piece of wood or the like,
the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions would become useless;
for it is observed that an agent cannot be prompted to act by his own intellect alone.

It is said: By means of the body, senses, and so forth, bestowed by the Supreme Lord, and empowered by Him alone, the individual soul (jīva)— serving as their substratum and possessing the powers imparted by Him— presides over the body, senses, and so forth by His own will for the accomplishment of karma.

But since the Supreme Lord, dwelling within all of that, grants His consent and impels it, there is no objection whatsoever to the fact that the individual soul possesses the capacity for activity and cessation through its own intellect;
the author of the Sūtras has determined this very point in such passages as "From the Supreme, because of the scriptural statement regarding those respective powers" (2.3.40).
If it is argued that the liberated soul (jīva) would lack agency because of the departure of the body, senses, and vital breaths, we say no;
for at that time, those divine [faculties] exist, perfected by its own volition (saṅkalpa). //14//
Whatever action a person undertakes with his body, speech, and mind— whether it be righteous or its opposite— these five are its causes. (18.15)
Śrīdhara: He states that these alone are the causes of all action in the verse beginning with "śarīra.
Action undertaken by means of the five aforementioned factors must be subsumed within these three;
for it is well known that action is threefold—bodily, vocal, and mental—as expressed by the phrase "by body, speech, and mind."
Whatever action—whether righteous or unrighteous—a person performs by means of the body and so forth, these five are the causes of that action.
Viśvanātha: Regarding the phrase "by means of the body and so forth," action is threefold: bodily, vocal, and mental;
and all of that is twofold.
That which is proper is righteous (*dharmya*), while that which is contrary is improper (*anyāyya*) and unrighteous (*adharmya*). These five causes apply to all such action.
Baladeva: Regarding the term "body" (*śarīra*)—that which is proper is according to the scriptures (*śāstrīya*).
The opposite is unscriptural. // 15 //
This being so, he who, due to an unrefined intellect, perceives the self alone as the sole agent, does not see; he is of perverted understanding. (18.16)
Śrīdhara: What follows from that? To this he says, "therein" (tatra). That is to say, in all action, these five are the causes.

This being so, he who perceives the Self—which is indeed devoid of attributes and unattached—as an agent due to an unrefined intellect resulting from the teachings of the scriptures and the preceptor, is of perverted understanding and does not see correctly.
Viśvanātha: What follows from that? To this he says: "In that regard" (tatra).

In this regard, since these five alone are the causes for every action, he who perceives the self— the individual soul— which is in reality entirely free from attachment, as the agent, is of wicked intellect because his understanding is characterized by egoism and lacks refinement; the sense is that such an ignorant person is called nothing but a blind man.
Baladeva: What follows from that? To this he says: "Therein.
Regarding the word "therein":
This being so— that the individual soul (jīva) is an agent only when preceded by the permission of the Supreme Lord and dependent upon the body and other factors granted by Him—
he who perceives the self, the jīva alone, as the sole agent in that action,
is of perverted intellect; because his understanding is unrefined and he has not attained knowledge, he does not see, just like a blind man.
He whose state of being is not characterized by egoism, and whose intellect is not tainted— even having slain these worlds, he does not slay, nor is he bound. (18.17)
Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry, "Who then is Sumati, of whom it was said that he has no taint of action? he says: "Of whom" (yasya).
"Made by the ego-sense" (ahaṅkṛta) means a state of being such as "I am the doer. Alternatively, "made by the ego-sense" refers to the state or nature of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
The meaning is that he has no attachment to agency,
because he perceives that the body and so forth alone are the agents of action;
for this very reason, his intellect is not defiled and he does not cling to actions with thoughts of "desirable" or "undesirable."

One who perceives the Self as distinct from the body and so forth does not kill even after slaying all these worlds and living beings when viewed from the perspective of the world; for, by virtue of his own vision, he remains detached and is not bound—meaning he does not incur bondage through the fruits of that action.

How much less, then, could there be any suspicion of bondage for him through those actions which, by means of purifying the mind, serve as causes for the arising of indirect knowledge (parokṣa-jñāna)? This is the meaning.
Thus it has been said: "He who performs actions by placing them in Brahman, having abandoned attachment, is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water" (Gītā 5.10).
Viśvanātha [comments]: To the question, "Who then is the wise one, the one with sight? he says, "Of whom... (yasya).

One who is free from "I-making"—that is, one whose state of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), nature, and attachment to agency do not exist, and for whom, for that very reason, the intellect is not smeared and does not become attached to actions through the notion of "desirable" or "undesirable"—he indeed does not obtain the fruit of action. What, then, is to be done? For he, even while performing good or evil deeds, truly does nothing at all; thus [the Lord] says, "Even having slain... and so forth.
Even though he has killed all these living beings from the perspective of worldly view (*loka-dṛṣṭi*), he does not kill them at all from his own perspective (*sva-dṛṣṭi*).
The sense is that this is because he is free from intentional motivation (*nirabhisandhitva*).
Therefore, he is not bound; he does not incur the fruit of karma.
Baladeva: To explain who, then, possesses vision and is wise, he says "of whom" (yasya).

That person whose state of being—characterized by the activity of the mind—is not egoistic (*ahaṅkṛta*) when his own agency is understood to be dependent on the Supreme Lord; that is, one for whom there arises no conceit such as "I alone am performing the actions";
and whose intellect is not stained by a longing for the fruits of action.
Having slain these worlds, as well as Bhīṣma and the others, he does not kill them [in reality], nor is he bound or tainted by that act of slaying all the worlds. // 17 //
Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower—this is the threefold impulse to action.
The instrument, the action, and the agent—this is the threefold aggregate of action. (18)
Śrīdhara: In order to establish precisely this— that "even having slain, one does not slay, nor is one bound"— with the intention that because the injunction for action,

the locus of action, and the fruits of action and so forth are composed of the three *guṇas*, the *ātman*, which is devoid of *guṇas*, has no connection with them, he speaks of the injunction for action and the locus of action [in the verse beginning] with "knowledge."
Knowledge is the cognition that "this is a means to achieve the desired";
the object of knowledge is the action that is a means to achieve the desired;
the knower is the substratum of such knowledge.

Thus, there are three kinds of impulsion toward action (*karma-codanā*). It is called "impulsion" (*codanā*) because by means of it one is impelled or set in motion. The meaning is that the triad beginning with knowledge (*jñāna*) is the cause for the engagement in action.
Alternatively, *codanā* is said to mean an injunction (*vidhi*).
As the Bhaṭṭas have stated: "The terms *codanā*, *upadeśa*, and *vidhi* are synonymous.

Consequently, the meaning is this: the injunction regarding ritual action (*karma-vidhi*) proceeds by taking as its basis the triad of knowledge and so forth, which possesses the aforementioned characteristics and consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*).

Thus it has been said: "The Vedas have the three *guṇas* as their subject matter. Likewise, the instrument (*karaṇa*) is that which is most effective in accomplishing an action, and the object (*karman*) is that which is most desired by the agent.
The agent (*kartṛ*) is that which brings about an action. That in which an object (*karman*) is contained is called "the collection of objects" (*karma-saṅgraha*).
The instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth constitute the threefold set of factors of action (*kāraka*).
The meaning is that [the agent] is the substratum of the action (*kriyā*).
However, the triad of factors beginning with the recipient (*sampradāna*) merely instigates the action through mutual relation;
they are not, however, the direct substratum of the action.
Therefore, it has been stated that only the triad beginning with the instrument (karaṇa) is the locus of action.
Viśvanātha: Thus, according to the opinion of the Blessed One, renunciation (saṃnyāsa) for the knowers of truth is indeed the sattvic form of abandonment characterized as previously described;
however, for devotees, the abandonment of karma-yoga is understood to be by its very nature.
As it was stated by the Blessed One himself in the Eleventh [Book]:
He who, having fully understood both virtues and faults— even those duties prescribed by me that pertain to himself— renounces them all;
"He who would worship Me, even having abandoned his own duties prescribed by Me in the form of the Vedas, he indeed is the best of beings.

The meaning of this was explained by the venerable Svāmī-pāda as follows: "He who would worship Me, even having abandoned his own duties prescribed by Me in the form of the Vedas, he indeed is the best of beings.
Is this [the case] due to ignorance or from atheism?

Having understood the virtues such as the purification of the being that result from practicing dharma, as well as the defects and transgressions in its opposite, one should abandon dharmas with a firm conviction that "by my devotion alone everything will be accomplished," even if this leads to distraction from my meditation;
in this context, the interpretation that "one should abandon the fruits of dharma" for the word *dharmān* is not tenable.
It should be noted that there is no sin incurred here in the renunciation of the fruits of one's actions (*dharma-phala-tyāga*).
This is the underlying meaning of the words of the Blessed One and of His commentators: knowledge certainly requires the purification of the mind (*citta-śuddhi*);
and only when the gradations of mental purity have been established through desireless actions (*niṣkāma-karma*) will the gradations of the arising of knowledge occur, and not otherwise.

Therefore, for the sake of achieving the arising of perfect knowledge, even renunciants must certainly perform action without desire. As it has been said: "For the sage who seeks to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means."
"For that very person who has ascended to yoga, tranquility is said to be the means" (Gītā 6.2).
But he who should be one who rejoices only in the Self...
"And the person who is satisfied in the Self,
and who finds contentment in the Self alone— for him there exists no duty to be performed" (Gītā 3.17).
But supreme, independent, and exceedingly powerful devotion does not depend upon the purification of the mind, as it is said:
"He who with faith hears this pastime of Viṣṇu performed by the women of Vraja," and so forth.
"Having obtained supreme devotion for the Blessed One, the wise man quickly casts off desire, that disease of the heart, in no long time. (BhP 10.33.42).

Here, however, when the qualified seeker possesses the disease of the heart by means of self-realization (*ātma-pratyaya*), even supreme devotion enters first; thereafter, within that very state, desire and the other afflictions depart. Thus...
Having entered the lotus of his own devotees' hearts through the aperture of the ear,
Kṛṣṇa shakes off their impurities.

And as it is said: "Just as [the clarity] of water [is restored] by autumn" (BhP 2.8.5). Therefore, if such purification of the mind occurs through devotion alone, then how should devotees perform ritual action?
Now let us return to the subject at hand: moreover, knowledge is not merely the cognition of the Self as distinct from the body and so forth;
rather, the true nature of the Self must also be known, and it is precisely one who possesses such knowledge who is a "knower" (jñānī).
However, this connection with action exists within the triad [of body, speech, and mind].
He says "knowledge" (jñāna) to indicate that even this must be understood by renunciants;
here, the word *codanā* denotes an injunction (*vidhi*).

Regarding what was stated by the Bhaṭṭas—that *codanā*, *upadeśa*, and *vidhi* are synonymous—the half-verse is explained by [the author] himself: "The instrument" (*karaṇam*) refers to that knowledge which is the instrumental factor (*kāraka*). This is because of the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is that by which something is known (*jñāyate*).
That which is to be known—the reality of the individual self (jīvātman)—is itself the causal factor of action (karma-kāraka).
He who is its thorough knower is the agent (kartā); thus, the meaning is that there are three types of causal factors (kārakas): the instrument (karaṇa), the object (karman), and the agent (kartā).
The "comprehension of action" means that it is comprehended precisely through the performance of action free from desire; this is the word-by-word explanation of the injunction regarding action.
The underlying sense is that these three—being the knower, being the object of knowledge, and being the act of knowing—are rooted in the performance of action free from desire. (18–19)

Baladeva: Just as in the *jñāna-kāṇḍa*, the triad of knowledge and so forth also exists in the *karma-kāṇḍa*. He teaches that this must be understood by one who is devoted to action (*karmaṭha*) while remaining established in [the Self], stating: "Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower"—thus the injunction for action (*karma-codanā*), such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and other ritual prescriptions, is endowed with this triad. For it is said by the learned: "Injunction (*codanā*), instruction (*upadeśa*), and prescription (*vidhi*) are synonymous."
That triad explains itself as "the instrument" (*karaṇa*).
According to etymology (*nirukti*), that which is knowledge is the instrument, in the sense that "it is known by means of this"; thus, the meaning is the instrumental factor (*kāraka*).
That which is to be known and performed, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and so forth, is the objective factor (*karma-kāraka*).
But he who is known as the one who performs it through its complete execution is the "agent" (kartṛ); thus, the agent-factor (kartṛ-kāraka) is established.

In this way, the collection of actions—such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and other ritual injunctions—is threefold, being accomplished by the triad of factors beginning with the instrument (karaṇa). This is the identical meaning of the two terms "injunction" (codanā) and "collection" (saṅgraha). // 18 //

Knowledge, action, and the agent—these three are indeed described according to the distinction of the qualities (guṇas) in the enumeration of the qualities; hear about them also as they truly are. 18.19.
Śrīdhara: What follows from that? To this he says: "Knowledge" (jñānam).
That in which the qualities (guṇas) are enumerated—that is, explained and established—through their various specific effects is the *Guṇasaṅkhyāna*, the Sāṅkhya scripture.
In that regard, knowledge, action, and the agent are each said to be of exactly three kinds, according to the distinctions among the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest.
Listen duly to those very things—knowledge and so forth—which are about to be described.

The emphatic particle "exactly" (*eva*) in the phrase "of exactly three kinds" is intended to exclude the notion that the Self possesses actions inherently, apart from the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the three qualities.
In the fourteenth chapter, by the passage beginning with "Therein, sattva, because of its purity," the manner in which the *guṇas* act as bonds is described.

In the seventeenth chapter, by the description of the threefold nature produced by the *guṇas* starting with "The *sāttvika*s worship the gods," it is stated that one should abandon the nature of *rajas* and *tamas* and cultivate a *sāttvika* nature through the practice of *sāttvika* food and other such things.

However, in this context, the distinction should be understood as follows: it is stated that all things consist of the three *guṇas* in order to demonstrate that there is no connection with the self (*ātman*) regarding action, its factors, the fruit, and so forth. //19//

Baladeva: It should be understood that in the fourteenth chapter, which enumerates and defines the *guṇas*, the manner in which the *guṇas* act as bonds was explained through verses such as "Sattva, because of its purity...
(14.7). Furthermore, in the seventeenth chapter, the distinctions in nature caused by the *guṇas* were stated through verses such as "The *sāttvika*s worship the gods...
(17.4). Here, however, the threefold nature of knowledge and the other faculties—termed *guṇas*—is being described. //19//
That knowledge by which one perceives the one undecaying reality in all beings, as undivided within the divided, know that to be *sāttvika*. (18.20)

Śrīdhara: Regarding that, he describes the threefold nature of knowledge—sāttvika and so forth—in three verses beginning with "sarva-bhūteṣu. By means of which knowledge one perceives—that is, discerns—the undivided, pervasive, single, imperishable, and changeless reality (bhāva), namely the essence of the Supreme Self (paramātma-tattva), within all beings, from Brahmā down to the stationary objects, even though they are divided and mutually distinct.
Know that knowledge to be of the nature of sattva. // 20 //
Viśvanātha states the knowledge pertaining to *sattva*: "In all beings...

[He perceives] the one state—the single individual self (*jīvātman*)—which, for the sake of experiencing various kinds of fruits, exists sequentially within all beings, such as humans, gods, animals, and so forth; which is imperishable, remaining undecaying even among those that are perishable; and which is undivided, even among those that are divided.
That knowledge by which one perceives all things—even though they are mutually distinct—as undivided and of a single form through their connection with action, is *sāttvika* knowledge. //20//

Baladeva explains sattvic knowledge: "In all beings," etc. That by which the individual self (jīvātman) is perceived as one—existing sequentially through the experience of the fruits of various actions within the bodies of all beings, such as gods and humans; that by which it is perceived as imperishable, being non-perishing amidst those perishable things; and that by which it is perceived as undivided and of a single form amidst those divided and mutually distinct things—that is sattvic knowledge, the knowledge of the undifferentiated Self according to the Upaniṣads.
The meaning is "that. //20//
But that knowledge which perceives various distinct entities as separate from one another in all beings— know that knowledge to be rajasic. (18.21)
Śrīdhara: He describes *rājasa* knowledge with the words "pṛthaktvena" (as distinct).
This is an elaboration of the very statement "yaj jñānaṃ pṛthaktvena" (that knowledge which [perceives] as distinct).

That knowledge by which one perceives—in all beings—the various states as being in fact multiple *kṣetrajñas* (individual souls), distinguished from one another in the form of happiness, suffering, and so forth, is *rājasa* knowledge.
Know that to be rajasic. //21//
Viśvanātha: He describes the *rājasa* knowledge as "that knowledge which [perceives] the individual self (*jīvātman*) as distinct from all beings.

The view of the *asuras* is that the destruction of the body is itself the destruction of the self; therefore, they hold that the self is indeed distinct and separate in each different body. Thus, because of their composition of various scriptures, they possess diverse types of views and manifold intentions.
The self is the substratum of pleasure and pain;
it is not the substratum of pleasure, pain, and so forth; it is insentient; it is sentient; it is all-pervasive;
it is of the nature of *a* and *ū*.
That by which one perceives "many" as "one," and so forth, is of the nature of passion (rājasa). //21//
Baladeva: He describes *rājasa* knowledge with the words "as distinct" (*pṛthaktvena*).

This refers to that knowledge which perceives the individual selves within all beings—that is, within the bodies of gods, humans, and so forth—as being separate [from one another], meaning the knowledge that the destruction of the body is itself the destruction of the self;
and by which one perceives various kinds of dispositions (*bhāva*) or intentions.

The knowledge by which one understands the doctrines of the Lokāyatas, Jains, Buddhists, Māyins, logicians (Tārkikas), and others—such as that the body itself is the self; that the self is distinct from the body and is of the same size as the body; that momentary consciousness is the self; that the self is eternal, pure consciousness alone, and all-pervading; or that the self is distinct from the body, is non-inert, all-pervading, and the substratum of the nine specific qualities—is *rājasa* knowledge. //21//
But that which is attached to a single task as if it were the whole, which is motiveless,
devoid of the true goal, and trivial— that is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). //22//

Śrīdhara: He states that [knowledge] characterized by *tamas* is "that which..."—namely, that which is joined with the dogmatic insistence (*abhiniveśa*) that in a single effect, such as the body or an image, the Self or Lord is "all-encompassing" (*kṛtsnavat*), as if complete (*paripūrṇavat*), thinking "this much alone is the Self or Lord"; which is without cause (*ahaituka*), meaning lacking logical justification;
and which does not possess the true object (*atattvārthavat*), being devoid of reliance upon the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, it is slight and trivial,
because its object is limited and its fruit is meager.
Knowledge that is of such a nature is declared to be tamasic. //22//

Viśvanātha: He describes tamasic knowledge as that knowledge which is without cause and merely innate; therefore, it is attached only to worldly activities—such as bathing, eating, drinking, sexual intercourse, and the means for those—and not to Vedic rites such as sacrifice and charity.
Therefore, the meaning is that there is no reality whatsoever in that which possesses the nature of non-reality.
That knowledge which is meager and trivial, like that of the beasts, is tāmasa;
whereas the knowledge of the referent of the word "That" (tat-pada) as being distinct from the body and so forth is sāttvika.

In brief, knowledge of the systems of logic and other sciences that propounds various doctrines is rajasic; knowledge concerning worldly affairs such as bathing, eating, and so forth is tamasic. //22//
Baladeva: He describes tamasic knowledge with the words "But that which... That knowledge which is causeless and innate, rather than knowledge derived from the authority of the scriptures;
therefore, it pertains to a single worldly activity such as bathing, eating, or sexual dalliance.
But in the case of Vedic sacrifices, charity, and so forth, it is not attached; rather, it is complete (*kṛtsnavat*) and full, meaning there is nothing superior to it.

For this very reason, that knowledge which is like something non-essential—wherein no essential reality exists—and which is meager and trivial because it is common to animals and the like, such as knowledge of worldly bathing, eating, and so on, is *tāmasa*. //22//
Action that is prescribed, performed without attachment and free from passion and hatred by one who does not desire the fruit— that is said to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika). //23//
Śrīdhara: Now he describes the threefold action with the three verses beginning with "niyatam" (regulated). "Regulated" means prescribed as a constant duty;
"free from attachment" means devoid of personal involvement or obsession.

That which is performed without attachment or aversion— neither out of affection for sons and the like nor out of hatred for enemies— and by an agent who is free from desire, seeking no fruit, such action is called *sāttvika*. //23//

Viśvanātha: Having described the threefold knowledge, he speaks of the threefold action: that action which is performed as a constant duty (*niyata*), ordained by eternal law, free from attachment—that is, devoid of personal investment—and therefore performed without passion or aversion, by an agent who is entirely devoid of desire for fruit; such action is *sāttvika*. (23)
Baladeva: Now, he describes the threefold nature of action with the three verses beginning with "niyatam.
"Niyatam" means prescribed for one's own varna and āśrama;
"saṅga-rahitam" means devoid of attachment and free from the obsession of being the doer.

That action which is performed without attachment or aversion, that which is not done out of passion for fame nor out of hatred for infamy, but rather as an offering to the Lord by one who desires no fruit and is devoid of longing for results—that is *sāttvika*. //23//
But that action which is performed by one desiring rewards, or again with egoism, and with great effort, is declared to be rajasic. (18.24)

Śrīdhara: He describes the *rājasa* action with the words "that which... (*yat*). However, that action which is performed by one desiring objects of desire—that is, wishing to obtain a fruit—by one possessed of egoism, and by one endowed with a deeply rooted egoism such as "Who else is a *śrotriya* equal to me?", and furthermore, that which involves great exertion and excessive affliction—that action is declared to be *rājasa*. //24//
Viśvanātha: "By one desiring [worldly] objects" means by one possessing little ego; "by one with ego" means by one possessing excessive ego. //24//

Baladeva: That action which is performed by a person who desires objects of longing, who seeks results, who is possessed of egoism, and who is intent upon the sense of agency, and which involves great exertion and excessive suffering—that is *rājasa*. (24)
That action which is undertaken out of delusion, without regard for its consequences, its loss, its violence, or one's own human capacity, is said to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). 18.25
Śrīdhara: He describes tamasic action with the word "anubandham. That which is bound to follow is "anubandha," meaning future good or evil; "kṣayam" means the depletion of wealth.
That action which is undertaken solely out of delusion, without regard for violence—that is, the infliction of pain on others—or for one's own human capacity, is said to be tāmasa. //25//

Viśvanātha: After the performance of ritual action (*anu-karma-anuṣṭhāna*), that which is undertaken out of delusion—that is, through ignorance alone—without regard for future bondage such as imprisonment by kings, robbers, or the messengers of Yama; for decline, meaning the diminution of virtue, knowledge, and so forth; and for injury, meaning one's own destruction—that worldly activity, which is to be performed merely by a worldly person, is *tāmasa*. (25)
Baladeva: Following the performance of ritual acts (*anu-karma*), there is bondage caused by royal messengers and the messengers of Yama;
decay, which is the destruction of merit and so forth;
and violence, which is the infliction of pain upon living beings.
That action which is undertaken out of delusion, without regard for one's own capacity or strength, is tāmasa. //25//

One who is free from attachment, devoid of the sense of "I," endowed with fortitude and enthusiasm, and remains unshaken by success or failure— such an agent is said to be characterized by goodness (sāttvika). 18.26
Śrīdhara: With three verses beginning with "mukta-saṅga," he describes the threefold agent.
"Mukta-saṅga" means one who has abandoned attachment;
"anahaṃvādī" means one devoid of boastful speech.
Fortitude is steadfastness; enthusiasm is exertion. Endowed with these means being joined with them.
One who remains unchanging in both the success and failure of an action undertaken, being free from joy and dejection—such an agent is said to be characterized by sattva. //26//
Viśvanātha: Karma has been described as being of three kinds; he now states that the agent is likewise of three kinds by saying, "one who is free from attachment" (mukta-saṅga). //26//
Baladeva: Now, with three verses beginning with "mukta," he describes the threefold nature of the agent.
One who is "freed from attachment" is devoid of the obsession with agency and the desire for its fruits.
One who is "free from egoistic speech" is devoid of boastful talk.
Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the endurance of unavoidable suffering until the completion of an undertaking.

Zeal (*utsāha*) is the state of a mind intent upon its execution. One who is endowed with these two remains unchanging—free from both pleasure and pain—whether the incidental result is achieved or not.
Such an agent is characterized by goodness (sāttvika). //26//
One who is passionate, desirous of the fruits of action, greedy, violent by nature, impure, and possessed by joy and grief— such an agent is proclaimed to be rajasic. (18.27)

Śrīdhara: He describes the passionate agent as "one who is full of attachment" (*rāgī*); that is, one who has affection for sons and so forth. "One who desires the fruit of action" (*karma-phala-prepsuḥ*) means one who longs for the results of action.
Greedy, longing for the wealth of others;
violent by nature, having a murderous disposition;
and possessed of joy and sorrow according to gain and loss—such an agent is proclaimed to be rajasic. //27//
Viśvanātha: "Rāgī" means attached to ritual action;
"lubdha" means attached to sense objects. //27//
Baladeva says: "One who is passionate" (rāgī) is one who is attached to wife, children, and so forth;

"one who desires the fruits of action" (karma-phala-prepsuḥ) is one who intensely longs for cattle, children, food, heaven, and the like; "one who is greedy" (lubdhaḥ) is one who is unable to spend the wealth required for ritual actions.
One who is violent by nature, performing actions that cause suffering to others;

who is impure, being devoid of the prescribed purification required for the action; and who is possessed by joy and sorrow at the success or failure of the fruit of his action—such an agent is characterized by passion (rājasa). //27//
The one who is undisciplined, vulgar, stubborn, deceitful, malicious, and lazy; who is despondent and a procrastinator—such a doer is said to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). 18.28
Śrīdhara: He describes the tamasic agent with the words "the undisciplined" (ayukta). "Undisciplined" means lacking attentiveness; "vulgar" (prākṛta) means devoid of discrimination.
"Stabdha" means unbending;
"śaṭha" means one who conceals his own power;
"naikṛtika" means one intent on cutting off the livelihood of others.

The indolent person is by nature disinclined to activity; even regarding what ought to be done, he is always dejected in disposition. Furthermore, the procrastinator is one who delays his duties for a long time, being always slow by nature;
that which should be done today or tomorrow, he does not perform even after a month.
And he who is such as this is called a tamasic agent. //28//
By the threefold nature of the agent, the threefold nature of the knower is also stated; and by the threefold nature of the object, the threefold nature of the knowable is likewise to be understood.
By the threefold nature of the intellect, the threefold nature of the instrument will also be stated. //28//

Viśvanātha: "The ill-mannered" (*ayukta*) means one who acts improperly; "the vulgar" (*prākṛta*) means one who remains within his own nature (*prakṛti*), that is, his own inherent disposition (*sva-svabhāva*).
The meaning is that he performs whatever comes to his own mind, and does not even regard the words of his teacher as authoritative.
A deceitful person is one who causes insult to others.

Therefore, in this way, only renunciation characterized as described by the knowers should be performed; only knowledge established in action that is characterized as *sāttvika* should be resorted to; only action that is *sāttvika* should be performed;
and one must become only a *sāttvika* agent.
This alone is the renunciation of the wise; this is my knowledge, the essential conclusion of the meaning of this section.

For the devotees, however, knowledge is indeed beyond the three modes of nature, their action is called the yoga of devotion and is beyond the three modes, and the performers are themselves beyond the three modes.
As it was said by the Blessed Lord himself in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam:
Isolation is sattvic knowledge,
while that which is characterized by doubt is rajasic;
knowledge pertaining to primordial nature is tamasic.
"It is remembered as being centered in the person and devoid of qualities" (BhP 11.25.24);
"Thus has the definition of *bhakti*-yoga, which is indeed beyond the modes of nature, been declared" (BhP 3.29.11).
The agent who is free from attachment is considered *sāttvika*;
the one blinded by passion is considered *rājasa*;
and the one whose memory is lost is considered *tāmasa*.
"He is devoid of qualities and takes refuge in Me" (BhP 11.25.26).
Furthermore, it is not only this triad that transcends the qualities (*guṇātīta*) in the perspective of devotion; rather, everything related to devotion transcends the qualities.
As it is said in that very same place:
Faith directed toward the self is characterized by sattva;
faith in ritual action is characterized by rajas;
and that faith which is in unrighteousness belongs to tamas.
"But in service to Me, they are devoid of qualities" (BhP 11.25.27). Furthermore, "Dwelling in the forest is said to be sattvic,
while dwelling in a village is called rājasic."
"The gambling hall is characterized by tamas, but my abode is devoid of the gunas. Thus [it is said].
Sattvic happiness arises from the Self.
"That which arises from sense objects is rājasa;
that which arises from delusion and dejection is tāmasa;
and that which is devoid of qualities and takes refuge in Me is [sāttvika]. (BhP 11.25.29) Thus it is said.
Thus, for devotees who have transcended the modes, all things related to their devotion—such as knowledge, action, faith, and their own happiness—are entirely beyond the modes.

For those in the mode of goodness who possess knowledge, all things related to that knowledge are purely of the nature of goodness. For those in the mode of passion who perform ritual actions, all such things are purely of the nature of passion.

It should be understood from the perspective of the meaning of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam and the Bhagavad-gītā that all those [actions] of unrestrained people dominated by ignorance (tāmasa) are themselves purely tāmasa.

Furthermore, it is stated in the fourteenth chapter that even for the wise, transcendence of the modes occurs only through exclusive devotion (bhakti) remaining after the renunciation of knowledge (jñāna-saṃnyāsa) in their final stage. //28//
Baladeva: "Improper" means acting in an unseemly manner.

"Prākṛta" means abiding in one's nature (prakṛti), that is, in one's own disposition; the meaning is that he performs actions solely according to his own nature, and not in accordance with the scriptures.
Stabdha means one who is unbending and insincere; śaṭha means one who conceals his own power; naikṛtika means one who causes humiliation to others;
and alasa means one who is lax regarding an undertaking once it has begun.
One who is dejected and overwhelmed by grief,
a procrastinator who does not perform what ought to be done in a single day even after a year—
such a doer is characterized by tamas. (28)
O Dhanañjaya, hear now from me the threefold division of the intellect and of fortitude according to the gunas, being described in their entirety and in their distinctness. (18.29)
Śrīdhara: Now he declares the threefold nature of both intelligence (buddhi) and fortitude (dhṛti) with the words "the division of intelligence" (buddher bhedaṃ).
The meaning is clear. //29//

Viśvanātha: In order to make it known that even those who possess knowledge (*jñānin*) should accept only that which is characterized by goodness (*sāttvika*), he states the threefold nature of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other faculties as well, beginning with the words "of the intellect" (*buddheḥ*). //29//

Baladeva: Having thus described the threefold nature of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower, he promises to describe that same threefold nature of intelligence (*buddhi*) and fortitude (*dhṛti*) with the words "of intelligence" (*buddheḥ*).
The meaning is clear. //29//

O Pārtha, that intellect which understands both engagement and withdrawal, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, fear and fearlessness, as well as bondage and liberation, is sattvic. 18.30.
Śrīdhara: Here, with three verses beginning with "pravṛttiṃ ca," he describes the threefold nature of the intellect (buddhi):
engagement (pravṛtti) in dharma and withdrawal (nivṛtti) from adharma.
That intellect which knows the internal organ—that is, that which discerns what action is to be done and what is not to be done in a particular place and time;

what constitutes fear and what is fearless; what is beneficial and what is harmful as determined by the performance or non-performance of action; and how bondage arises or how liberation occurs—that intellect is *sāttvika*.
