Although it should have been stated as "that by which a person knows," the agentive case is used for the instrument, as in the expression "the pieces of wood cook. //30//
Viśvanātha: Fear and fearlessness have their causes in saṃsāra and the absence of saṃsāra. //30//
Baladeva: Regarding this, he describes the threefold nature of the intellect with the three verses beginning with "pravṛttiṃ ca.

That intellect which knows engagement in dharma and withdrawal from adharma—where it should have been said "by which one knows," the agency is metaphorically attributed to the instrument [the intellect].
Just as in the expression "the axe cuts," he who knows what ought to be done and what ought not to be done—

understanding that action performed without desire is to be done while action performed with desire is not to be done— and who knows fear and fearlessness, understanding that there is fear from activity contrary to the scriptures but fearlessness from activity in accordance with the scriptures; [he is a man of knowledge].
That intellect which knows bondage as the true nature of saṃsāra, and liberation as the true nature of its severance, is sāttvika. //30//
O Pārtha, that intellect by which one perceives dharma and adharma, as well as what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, incorrectly, is of the nature of passion (rājasī). 18.31.
Śrīdhara: He states the *rājasī* intellect with the words "yayā" (by which).
The meaning is: by that [intellect] which is improper, serving as a locus for doubt.
The rest is clear. //31//
Viśvanātha: "Inaccurately" means "without conviction. //31//
Baladeva: He describes the *rājasī* intellect with the words "yayā" (by which);
that is, by being improper (*ayathāvat*) and uncontrolled (*asamyatvena*). //31//
That intellect which, enveloped by darkness, perceives unrighteousness as righteousness and regards all things in a perverted manner— that, O Pārtha, is tāmasī intellect. (18.32)
Śrīdhara: He speaks of the *tāmasī* intellect with the words "unrighteousness" (*adharma*).
The meaning is that the intellect which perceives things erroneously is *tāmasī*.
Intellect (*buddhi*) is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) mentioned previously.
Knowledge, however, is a modification (vṛtti) of that [internal organ];
fortitude as well is indeed a modification of it.
Alternatively, since the internal organ is the substratum (dharmin), even the intellect (buddhi), characterized by determination (adhyavasāya), is simply its modification.

Although there are many such fluctuations as desire, aversion, and so forth, these three types are mentioned because they are predominant as the means for achieving dharma and adharma, or fear and fearlessness;
this is also an illustration that includes others. //32//
Viśvanātha: "That by which one thinks" means that by which one conceives [an object], just as in the expression "the axe cuts. //32//
Baladeva: He describes the *tāmasī* intellect with the words "unrighteousness" (*adharma*).
The meaning is that the intellect which perceives things erroneously is *tāmasī*. It perceives all objects perversely, taking the good to be bad, and the bad to be good.
The meaning is that he considers all things to be inverted, such as thinking the supreme reality is the inferior, and the inferior reality is the supreme. //32//
O Pārtha, that resolve by which one maintains the activities of the mind, the vital breaths, and the senses through unwavering yoga— that resolve is of the nature of goodness (sāttvikī). 18.33
Śrīdhara: Now, with three verses beginning with "By means of *dhṛti*," he describes the threefold nature of *dhṛti*.

That *dhṛti* by which one maintains—i.e., restrains—the activities of the mind, the vital breaths, and the senses through *yoga*, characterized by one-pointedness of mind and being non-deviating (not holding onto other objects), is *sāttvika* *dhṛti*. (33)
Viśvanātha: He states the threefold nature of fortitude (dhṛti) with the verse beginning "dhṛtyā" (33).
Baladeva: He explains the threefold nature of fortitude (dhṛti) with the following three verses beginning with "dhṛtyā.
That fortitude by which a person sustains the activities that serve as the means for the yoga of the mind, the vital breaths, and the senses, is sattvic.
To the question "Of what kind? he says: "By means of yoga.
Yoga is the contemplation of the Supreme Self; by that [yoga], which is non-deviating—that is, not grasping any other object—this is the meaning. //33//
But that resolve by which one holds fast to duty, pleasure, and wealth, O Arjuna,
desiring their fruits through attachment— that resolve, O Pārtha, is rajasic. (18.34)
Śrīdhara: He describes the *rājasī* fortitude with the words "But by which...

(*yayā tu*). That *rājasī* fortitude is that by which one holds fast to, and does not relinquish, virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*) as the primary goals; and through attachment to them, one becomes desirous of their fruits.
Viśvanātha—no comment. Baladeva: In connection with the learned person who possesses desires, [it refers to] the person who longs for results;
by means of which [devotion], he sustains dharma and the rest, as well as the activities of the mind, vital breath, and senses, which serve as the means for attaining those [results].
That resolve is of the nature of passion (rājasa),
by which one clings to sleep, fear, sorrow, despondency, and even intoxication. (BhG 18.35)
The dull-witted person does not relinquish it; that steadfastness, O Pārtha, is tāmasī.

Śrīdhara: He describes the *tāmasī* resolve (*dhṛti*) with the verse beginning "yayā. A person of dull intellect (*durmedhas*), whose intelligence is characterized by wickedness and a lack of discrimination, does not abandon sleep and the like through such a resolve, but rather returns to them again and again;
here, "sleep" refers to slumber—that resolve is *tāmasī*. (35)
Viśvanātha: No comment.
Baladeva: That resolve by which a person of dull intellect does not abandon dreams and the like, but rather clings to them, is tamasic resolve.
Dreaming is sleep;
intoxication is the pride born from the enjoyment of sense objects.

By the words "dreaming" and so forth, the activities of the mind, vital breath, and senses that cause those states are meant; that by which one maintains [the body] through these is the meaning of *tāmasī* fortitude. //35//
But now, O bull of the Bharatas, hear from me the threefold nature of happiness, wherein one finds delight through practice and reaches the end of suffering. (18.36)
That happiness which is like poison at first but like nectar in its result, born from the serenity of one's own intellect, is declared to be *sāttvika*. //37//
Śrīdhara: Now, with the half-verse beginning "Happiness," he declares the threefold nature of happiness;
the meaning is clear. (36)
Regarding that, he describes sattvic happiness with the verse beginning "from practice" (abhyāsāt).
In whatever happiness one delights through practice— that is, through extreme familiarity—
one does not attain delight all at once as is the case with sensual pleasure.
Delighting in which one reaches—that is, attains—the very end or cessation of suffering.
Of what nature is that?
It is that which, at first (*agre*), is like something unpleasant, as if bringing about suffering because it depends upon the restraint of the mind.
But in its final transformation, it is like nectar.
Intellect whose object is the Self is "self-intellect" (ātmabuddhi).
Its serenity (prasāda) is its abiding in clarity through the abandonment of the impurities of passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas).
The happiness born from that is declared by the yogis to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika). //37//
Viśvanātha—He describes sattvic happiness with one and a half verses: "One rejoices through practice," that is, through repeated cultivation, and not as one rejoices in sense objects by mere birth;
"one reaches the end of suffering" means that while rejoicing therein, one crosses over the suffering of saṃsāra. // 36 //
"Like poison" means that the cessation of the senses and the mind is indeed painful at first; such is the sense. //37//
Baladeva: Now, with the half-verse beginning "But happiness," he introduces the threefold nature of happiness.
Therein, with the one and a half verses beginning "From practice," he describes the *sāttvika* happiness:
that wherein one finds delight through "practice"—that is, through repeated cultivation.
But it is not by way of arising as it does with respect to sense objects;
for one who delights in this reaches the end of suffering and crosses over saṃsāra. // 36 //

That happiness which at first appears like poison—because it arises from the effort of restraining the mind and because it involves the illumination of the isolated Self—it seems to bring extreme suffering;
yet in its transformation, when concentration has reached maturity, it becomes like nectar due to that illumination of the isolated Self, like the falling of a stream of ambrosia.
And that which arises from the clarity of the intellect associated with the Self is *sāttvika* happiness.
And its clarity is the cessation of the impurity caused by connection with objects. //37//
That pleasure which arises from the contact of the senses with their objects, which is like nectar at first but like poison in its consequence, is declared to be rajasic. (18.38)
Śrīdhara: He describes rajasic happiness as "from the contact of objects," meaning that which is well-known as the pleasure derived from association with women and so forth;
it is like nectar at first—initially—but in its consequence it is equal to poison, because it is a cause of suffering both in this world and the next.
That happiness is said to be rajasic. //38//
Viśvanātha: That which is like nectar, such as sexual union with another's wife and so forth. //38//

Baladeva: That pleasure which, through the contact or connection of the senses—the eyes, ears, and so forth—with sense objects such as the form and touch of a young woman, is like nectar at first and exceedingly sweet, but in its final transformation—that is, at the conclusion—becomes like poison and brings extreme suffering because it is a cause for hell, is *rājasa* pleasure. (38)

That pleasure which is delusive to the self both at the beginning and in its consequence, arising from sleep, indolence, and negligence— that is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). //39//

Śrīdhara: He describes the *tāmasa* pleasure with the words "that which... and so forth. Furthermore, that pleasure which at the outset (*agre*)—in the first moment—and also subsequently (*anubandhe*) causes delusion (*moha-kara*) to the self, he explains as follows: sleep, laziness, and negligence (*pramāda*)—which is grasped by the mind through a lack of attention to what ought to be done—from these arises the pleasure; that is declared to be *tāmasa*. (39)
Viśvanātha: No commentary.

Baladeva: That which deludes the self—obscuring the true nature of reality—at its onset (during the time of experience), in its persistence (subsequently), and at its fruition (at the time of maturation), and which arises from sleep and the like—that is *tāmasa* happiness.
Laziness is the sluggishness of the functioning of the senses;
negligence is the absence of attention toward what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. //39//
There is no being on earth, or again in heaven among the gods, that is free from these three qualities born of material nature. (18.40)
Śrīdhara: Summarizing the meaning of the section even though it was not explicitly stated, he concludes with the words "not that" (*na tat*).

Whatever there may be—whether the multitude of living beings liberated from these three qualities (*guṇa*), such as *sattva* and the rest, which arise from *prakṛti*, or anything else—that is not [the Self].
The meaning is that it does not exist anywhere on earth, in the world of humans and so forth, nor in heaven among the gods. //40//

Viśvanātha: Summarizing the meaning of the section by including even what has not been explicitly stated, he says "no"—there is no such thing as a living being (*prāṇi-jātam*) or any other mere object whatsoever that could exist anywhere free from or devoid of these three qualities born of *prakṛti*; therefore, every collection of objects consists of the three qualities.
In this regard, the purport of the section is that only the *sāttvika* [type] is to be adopted, whereas the *rājasa* and *tāmasa* types are not to be adopted. //40//
Baladeva: Concluding the meaning of the section, he includes even what was not explicitly stated with the words "not that" (*na tad*).

On the earth—among humans and the like—in heaven—such as the celestial realm—and among the gods, within nature (*prakṛti*) when it is combined [with spirit], from Brahmā down to a blade of grass (*stamba*); this is the meaning.
That sentient being (*sattva*), the collection of living creatures, and other objects do not exist [independently].

That which would be free from or devoid of these three qualities born of nature—since, among things composed of the three qualities, only that which is of the nature of *sattva* is useful—it is precisely that which should be accepted, while the other should be abandoned; such is the meaning of the section. //40//
O scorcher of the foe, the duties of the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras have been divided according to the qualities born of their own natures. 18.41.

Śrīdhara: Now, if all this—action, the factors of action, their fruits, and the entire multitude of living beings—is indeed composed of the three *guṇas*, then how can there be liberation for this [being]?

In response to this inquiry, he begins another section to demonstrate the essential summary of the entire meaning of the *Gītā*: that liberation comes through the worship of the Supreme Lord by means of actions prescribed according to one's own specific qualification, and through the knowledge obtained by His grace.
"O Brāhmaṇa," and so on, until the end of the chapter:
O scorcher of foes, O tormentor of enemies!
The duties of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras have been distinctly ordained according to their specific divisions.

The separate treatment of the Śūdras is due, in brief, to their distinction from the twice-born by virtue of lacking that status. He states that this serves as an illustration of their classification: "by those qualities"—meaning those such as *sattva* and so forth—which "originate" or manifest from their respective natures (*svabhāva*).
Alternatively, *svabhāva* refers to the impressions (*saṃskāra*) from previous births.
Therefore, the meaning is "having manifested.
Kṣatriyas are those in whom rajas is predominant with sattva as a subordinate factor; vaiśyas are those in whom rajas is predominant with tamas as a subordinate factor.
Śūdras are those for whom darkness (tamas) is predominant and who have kings as their subordinates. //41//

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, he explains with six verses beginning with "brāhmaṇa" that even the multitude of living beings, though composed of the three *guṇas*, achieve their purpose by propitiating the Supreme Lord through prescribed actions performed according to their respective qualifications.

The meaning is that there are specific duties ordained for the Brāhmaṇas and others, which are clearly distinguished (*prakarṣeṇa vibhaktāni*) by those qualities—such as *sattva* and the rest—that manifest (*prabhavanti*) or appear by their very nature (*svabhāvena utpattyā*). //41//

Baladeva: Although all things are composed of the three *guṇas*, nevertheless, if Brahmins and others should perform their own prescribed duties with the disposition of worshiping the Lord, then those very duties will produce steadfastness in knowledge and become means of liberation; to state this, he begins the section with the six verses beginning with "The Brahmin... (*brāhmaṇa*).
The separate treatment of the Śūdras is due briefly to their lack of the status of the twice-born.
The duties of the four classes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, have been divided by the scripture along with the qualities arising from their own natures.
"Nature" (svabhāva) refers to past impressions; those qualities such as *sattva* and the rest which arise from it—along with these, their duties have been distinguished and declared by the scripture.

Thus, regarding those such as the Brāhmaṇas who possess these qualities, their respective functions are as follows: therein, the Brāhmaṇa is characterized primarily by *sattva* because of his tranquility; the Kṣatriya has *rajas* as predominant with *sattva* as subordinate because of his sovereign nature; the Vaiśya has *rajas* as predominant with *tamas* as subordinate because of his lack of preeminence here; and the Śūdra has *tamas* as predominant with *rajas* as subordinate because of his deluded nature.
But the ritual actions (karmāṇi) are to be discussed first. //41//
Tranquility, self-control, austerity, purity, forbearance, and uprightness, as well as knowledge, realization, and faith— these are the duties of a Brahmin, born of his own nature. (18.42)
Śrīdhara: Regarding that, he states the natural duties of a Brāhmaṇa as "tranquility" (śama) and so forth. Tranquility is the cessation of the mind;
self-control (dama) is the cessation of the external senses.
Austerity (tapas) refers to what was previously mentioned, such as the Śārīraka and other forms;
purity (śauca) is both external and internal;
and forbearance (kṣānti) is patience (kṣamā).
Uprightness is straightforwardness itself;
knowledge is theoretical understanding, and realized knowledge is experiential wisdom; faith is the state of being a believer, consisting of conviction in the meanings of the scriptures.
The "brahminical action" is the action of the brahmin caste arising from its own nature.
That which was stated as "they are distinguished by qualities originating from their own nature" is precisely what is meant by "arising from its own nature. //42//
Viśvanātha: Regarding that, he describes the natural duties (*svābhāvika-karmāṇi*) of the Brāhmaṇas, who are characterized by a predominance of *sattva*, beginning with "tranquility" (*śama*).

Tranquility is the restraint of the internal senses; self-control (*dama*) is the restraint of the external senses; austerity (*tapas*) pertains to the body and so forth; knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*) arise from the study of the scriptures and personal experience; and orthodoxy (*āstikya*) is firm conviction in the meaning of the scriptures. Such are the duties of a Brāhmaṇa, which constitute the path of Brahman (*brahma-karma*).
That which is born from the intrinsic nature of karma is the essential nature. //42//

Baladeva: He states that tranquility (*śama*) is the natural duty (*svābhāvika-karma*) of a Brāhmaṇa. Tranquility is the restraint of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); self-control (*dama*) is the restraint of the external organs; austerity (*tapas*) is bodily mortification according to the scriptures.
Purity is said to be twofold.
Patience is the capacity for endurance; straightforwardness is the absence of crookedness. Knowledge is the comprehension of the reality of the higher and the lower derived from the scriptures.
Therefore, from that very [knowledge] comes the certain realization of the Dharma:

that Hari, who is known through all the Vedas, is the sole cause of everything; and when propitiated by one's own performed actions and satisfied by unalloyed devotion (*bhakti*), He bestows everything up to His own self—such is the meaning established by the scriptures.
The ascertainment of truth:
this is the natural activity of Brahman.
Nevertheless, because of the predominance of the quality of *sattva*, it is designated as "the activity of the Brāhmaṇa."
Thus it was said by Viṣṇu:
"Forgiveness, truthfulness, self-restraint, purity, charity, and control of the senses."
Non-violence, service to the teacher, visiting sacred fords, and compassion.
Straightforwardness, freedom from greed, worship of the gods and Brahmins,
and likewise, the absence of malice.
This is called the generality of dharmas. //42//
Heroism, majesty, firmness, dexterity, and not fleeing in battle, as well as generosity and lordliness— this is the duty of the kṣatriya, born of his own nature. (18.43)
Śrīdhara: He states the natural duties of a Kṣatriya with the words "valor" and so forth. Valor is prowess;
*tejas* is boldness.
Fortitude is steadfastness;
skill is proficiency;
and in battle, it is also the refusal to flee, which is the state of not turning one's back.
Generosity is magnanimity;
sovereignty is the power of command.
This is the natural duty of a Kṣatriya. //43//

Viśvanātha: He describes the duties of the Kṣatriyas, for whom passion (rajas) is predominant with goodness (sattva) as a subordinate quality: "heroism" (śaurya) is valor; "splendor" (tejas) is boldness; "fortitude" (dhṛti) is steadfastness; "lordship" (īśvarabhāva) is the state of being the ruler of the world.
Baladeva: He states the duty of the Kṣatriya: "heroism" (śaurya).
Heroism is the fearless engagement in battle.
*Tejas* is invincibility against others. *Dhṛti* is the absence of exhaustion in body and senses even in great distress. *Dākṣya* is skill in the successful accomplishment of actions.
In battle, even when certain of one's own death, it is non-retreat and the absence of turning back;
generosity is the relinquishing of one's own wealth without hesitation;
and lordship is the manifestation of the power of authority over those subject to rule who transgress the commands, for the sake of protecting the subjects.
This is the natural duty of a Kṣatriya. //43//
Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are the duties of a Vaiśya, born of his own nature; likewise, service is the duty of a Śūdra, born of his own nature. (18.44)
Śrīdhara: He states the duties of the Vaiśya and the Śūdra with the words "agriculture" (*kṛṣi*) and so forth. *Kṛṣi* means plowing. One who protects cows is a *gau-rakṣa*.
The state of that [occupation] is *gaurakṣya*,
meaning cattle-rearing;
*vāṇijya* refers to buying, selling, and so forth.
This is the duty born of the nature of a Vaiśya;
likewise, that which consists of service to the three other castes is the duty born of the nature of a Śūdra as well. //44//
Viśvanātha: He describes the duty of those for whom *rajas* is predominant and *tamas* is subordinate as "agriculture" (*kṛṣi*).

A cowherd (*go-rakṣa*) is one who guards cows; his state is "cowherding" (*gaurakṣyam*). He describes the duty of the *śūdras*, for whom *tamas* is predominant and *rajas* is subordinate, as consisting of service (*paricaryātmakam*), that is, having the form of service toward the *brāhmaṇas*, *kṣatriyas*, and *vaiśyas*. //44//
Baladeva says: "For the Vaiśya, he states 'agriculture' (kṛṣi). Agriculture is the tilling of the earth with plows and other implements for the production of food and the like.
Animal husbandry (pāśupālya) is the protection of cattle."

The work of a merchant (*vaṇik-karma*) is trade (*vāṇijya*), characterized by buying and selling; the lending of wealth for the sake of interest is included here as well under the term *kuśīda*. This is indeed the duty of a Vaiśya, established by his very nature.
Now, regarding the Śūdra, he says "pari... [and so forth].

Service to those of twice-born origin, such as Brāhmaṇas and others, is the natural duty of the Śūdra. These [duties] are indicative of the duties belonging to the four stages of life (āśramas). //44//
Devoted to his own particular duty, a man attains perfection. Listen to how one who is intent on his own work finds success. 45.

Śrīdhara: He states that such actions as those of a Brāhmaṇa and others serve as causes for knowledge in the verse beginning with "sve sve" (in one's own). A person who is devoted to—that is, firmly established in—the action prescribed according to his own specific qualification attains *saṃsiddhi*, which is fitness for knowledge.
He explains the manner in which actions lead to the attainment of knowledge in the verse and a half beginning with "sva-karma" (one's own duty).
Listen to the manner in which one who has perfected their own karma attains the knowledge of reality, and the specific way by which it is attained. //45//
Viśvanātha: No commentary.
Baladeva: He states that the aforementioned actions are the cause of knowledge: "In their respective [duties]...

A person who is devoted to and performs the duties prescribed for his own particular caste and stage of life attains *saṃsiddhi*—that is, he reaches the state of steadfastness in knowledge which is inherent within those very actions, like a thread woven through a cloth.

If it is asked, "How can the culmination of knowledge, which liberates from actions that act as bonds, [be attained]? he says, "By one's own action," [referring to] a particular state of the intellect. //45//
From whom the activity of all beings proceeds, and by whom all this is pervaded— by worshipping Him through one's own duty, a human being attains perfection. 46.
Śrīdhara explains that very point with the words "yataḥ" (from whom):
from whom, that is, from the Supreme Lord who is the inner controller, the activity—that is, the movement—of living beings (*bhūta*) arises;
and by which [Lord], in the form of the cause, this entire universe is pervaded (*tataṃ*).
Having worshipped and honored that Lord with his own actions, a person attains perfection. //46//
Viśvanātha: From the Supreme Lord (yataḥ parameśvarāt).
By the phrase "having worshipped Him alone," worship of Him consists precisely in mentally offering that [action] to Him with the thought, "May the Supreme Lord be pleased by this action. //46//
Baladeva: "From whom" means from that Supreme Lord from whom the activity of living beings—characterized by birth and so forth—proceeds;
and by whom this entire world is pervaded, Him who exists in the form of deities such as Indra, [one should worship] with one's own prescribed [offering].

Having honored with this action, and having mentally dedicated that action to Him—the Lord of oneself—with the thought, "May my own Master be pleased," the human being attains perfection, which is steadfastness in knowledge. //46//
Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the duty of another well performed.
Performing the action prescribed by one's own nature, one incurs no sin. 47.
Śrīdhara: He states the purpose of the qualification "one's own duty" with the words "is better.
Even one's own duty, though deficient in its qualities, is better—that is, superior—to the duty of another, even if that other duty is perfectly performed.

Furthermore, it should not be thought that the duty of another, such as wandering for alms, is superior to one's own duty, such as battle, even when that battle involves the killing of kinsmen and the like.
For one who performs action as determined by necessity—that is, according to the aforementioned inherent nature—does not incur sin. //47//

Viśvanātha: Nor should one perform sattvic action out of a lack of interest in one's own duty upon seeing that it is rajasic due to its ritual aspects and so forth; thus he says, "Better is" (śreyān).

One's own duty (svadharma), even if deficient (viguṇa)—meaning inferior or impossible to perform correctly—is better than another's duty (paradharma), even if that other duty is excellent and well-performed.

The implication is that you should not abandon your own duty of battle—which, though possessing defects such as the killing of kinsmen—and instead adopt another's duty, such as wandering for alms. //47//

Baladeva: Now, if it is argued that since the duties of Kṣatriyas and others are characterized by *rajas* and so forth, those Kṣatriyas and others who lack interest in them should instead practice the *sāttvika* duty of Brahman, the Lord says in response: "Better is one's own duty," and so on.
One's own duty (*svadharma*), even if deficient or inferior, is better—that is, more highly praised—than the well-performed duty of another, because it has been ordained [by scripture].
O son of Kuntī, one should not abandon one's innate duty, even if it is flawed;
for all undertakings are enveloped by defect, as fire is by smoke. 48.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, if you consider that your own duty (*svadharma*) possesses the defect of violence according to the Sāṅkhya view, and thus regard another's duty (*paradharma*) as superior, then the presence of defects is equal even in the other's duty;
with this intention, he says: "Innate. One should not abandon innate action—that which is ordained by one's own nature—even if it is defective.
For indeed, all undertakings— all actions, whether for visible or invisible purposes— are pervaded and enveloped by some defect,
just as fire is enveloped by its innate smoke.

Therefore, just as one sets aside the defect of fire in the form of smoke and resorts to its very heat for the removal of darkness, cold, and so forth, even so, one should set aside the defective portion of action and resort to its virtuous portion alone for the purification of the *sattva*.
The meaning is "it is to be served. //48//
Viśvanātha: Nor should it be thought that there is fault only in one's own duty (*svadharma*), for there is indeed some fault even in the duties of others; thus he says, "Innate" (*sahajam*).
Since all undertakings—actions that are means for attaining the seen and the unseen—are indeed enveloped by fault, because they are innate, being ordained by one's own nature (*svabhāva*).
Just as fire, when shrouded by smoke, is perceived only through that defect;

therefore, having removed the defect in the form of smoke, its heat alone is utilized for the cessation of darkness, cold, and so forth—likewise, having abandoned the defective portion of action, its virtuous portion alone should be cultivated for the purification of the mind (sattva). This is the intended meaning. //48//

Baladeva: It is certainly not the case that only the duties of Kṣatriyas and others, such as warfare, are defective; nor are the duties of Brahmins likewise so. To this he says, "Innate" (*sahajam*). One should not abandon an action that is innate—that is, obtained by one's very nature—even if it is defective or mixed with violence; rather, because it is prescribed, one should indeed perform it.
The meaning is that one should perform the duties of a Brahmin with the understanding that they are faultless; for this reason, the text says "all.

The undertakings—that is, the actions—of all the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, are generally enveloped and pervaded by some defect because they consist of the three *guṇas* and are accomplished through material substances (*dravya*).
Just as fire is [perceived] through smoke, so too, having set aside the smoky portion of the fire, heat is resorted to for the sake of warding off cold and other such things.

Likewise, by dedicating actions to the Blessed One, one shakes off the portion consisting of defects; the intention is that the portion which generates knowledge for the sake of perceiving the Self is what should be cultivated. //48//
With an intellect unattached everywhere, having conquered the self and being free from longing,
one attains the supreme perfection of actionlessness through renunciation. (18.49)

Śrīdhara: Now, in response to the inquiry, "When action is being performed, how can it result in the very portion of excellence by abandoning the portion of defect? he says: "one whose intellect is unattached" (asakta-buddhiḥ). This means one whose intellect is devoid of attachment. "One who has conquered the self" (jitātmā) means one who is free from egoism (nirahaṅkāraḥ).
"Free from longing" means one from whom longing—the desire for results—has departed.
"Having thus abandoned attachment as well as the fruit, that renunciation is considered to be of the nature of *sattva*" (Gītā 18.9).

In this way, through the previously mentioned renunciation characterized by the abandonment of attachment to action and its fruit, he attains the perfection of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya-siddhi*), which is the purification of the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*) characterized by the cessation of all karma.

Although the performance of action through the renunciation of attachment and its fruit is indeed *naiṣkarmya* (freedom from action), because of the absence of any insistence on agency— as stated in the four verses beginning with, "The disciplined knower of truth should think, 'I do nothing at all'" (Gītā 5.8).

Nevertheless, by means of this renunciation characterized as described above, one attains the supreme perfection of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya-siddhi*), which is synonymous with the state of a *paramahaṃsa* and characterized by such statements as: "Having renounced all actions through the mind, the self-controlled one dwells in happiness" (Gītā 5.13). //49//

Viśvanātha: This being so, for that first renunciant who has abandoned the defects of action—characterized by the obsession with agency and the desire for fruits—the Lord speaks of a second kind of renunciation, which consists in the abandonment of actions even in their essential form, at the stage when he has ascended to yoga through the maturation of his practice over time: "With a mind unattached everywhere... (2.48).

He whose intellect is not attached to material objects and is free from attachment is therefore "one who has conquered the self," having brought the mind under control. He is "one whose longing has vanished" even for pleasures extending as far as the world of Brahmā.

Consequently, through renunciation—the abandonment of actions both in their outward form and in their essence—he attains, that is, reaches, the supreme and most excellent perfection of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya*).
The meaning is that in the state of one who has ascended to yoga, his freedom from action (naiṣkarmya) becomes an excellence of perfection. //49//

Baladeva: Thus, being one who desires to ascend [to the higher stage], one who is established in the discipline of knowledge—having realized his true nature through the discipline of action which contains that knowledge as its core—should then abandon the discipline of action in its essential form. To this effect, the Lord says: "With an unattached intellect... One whose intellect is unattached to all things other than the Self, because he is a "conquered self" (jitātmā)—his mind having been brought under control by the relish of the bliss of his own Self—and for that very reason "free from longing," being devoid of desire for the various kinds of pleasures achievable through objects other than the Self.

By the renunciation—that is, the abandonment in its true nature—of those actions that distract from the relish of the bliss of one's own Self, one who has ascended to yoga attains the supreme perfection characterized by actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya*). This very point was stated in the third chapter with the words beginning, "But he who should be delighted in the Self alone" (Gītā 3.17). //49//
Learn from me, O son of Kuntī, how one who has attained perfection reaches Brahman, and what the supreme culmination of knowledge is in brief. 50.

Śrīdhara: With six verses beginning with "Having attained perfection," [the Lord] describes the manner in which such a Paramahaṃsa attains the state of Brahman through steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*).
Having attained the perfection of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya-siddhi*), understand from my words in brief that manner—in which, by what method—he attains Brahman.
To demonstrate this very attainment of Brahman as it is firmly established, He says: "That which is the supreme culmination of knowledge."
The meaning is that "niṣṭhā" signifies the finality, the ultimate limit, and the completion. //50//
Viśvanātha: And thus, "in whatever way" (*yathā*) means by which manner one attains Brahman—that is, experiences Brahman.
That alone is the culmination (*niṣṭhā*) of knowledge; the meaning is that it is the supreme (*parā*) or ultimate limit (*paramo 'ntaḥ*).
According to Amara, *niṣṭhā* [denotes] completion, destruction, and end.

The meaning is: when ignorance has almost ceased and knowledge is beginning to arise, understand that manner by which one, having performed the renunciation of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃnyāsa*), may experience Brahman. //50//
Baladeva: Regarding the word "siddhim" (perfection):

having propitiated Hari by means of prescribed action, one attains that state of steadfastness in meditation on the Self which arises from His grace and culminates in the renunciation of all actions; then, in whatever manner one remains established therein, one attains Brahman—that is, one experiences one's own essential nature in which the eightfold qualities have been manifested.
Understand from me as I speak briefly of that manner;
and hear also that which I declare to you—the supreme culmination of knowledge, which has the Supreme Lord as its object. //50//

Endowed with a purified intellect and having restrained the self with fortitude, one should abandon the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, and cast off both attachment and aversion. (18.51)
Frequenting solitude, eating lightly, with speech, body, and mind restrained, he is constantly devoted to the yoga of meditation and has fully taken recourse to dispassion. //52//
Having abandoned egoism, power, arrogance, desire, anger, and possessiveness, one who is free from the sense of "mine" and tranquil is fit for becoming Brahman. 53.

Śrīdhara: Thus he says, "by means of the intellect" (*buddhyā*). In the manner described, being endowed with the aforementioned pure, *sāttvika* intellect, and having restrained that very intellect by means of *sāttvika* fortitude (*dhṛti*), making it steady, and having abandoned the objects such as sound and so forth—namely, attachment and aversion toward those objects—[one attains peace].
The connection of the words beginning with "having cast off by means of purified intellect" and ending with "is fit for becoming Brahman" is with the third [verse]. // 51 //
Furthermore, regarding the word "secluded" (*vivikta*):
one who frequents secluded places, dwells in a pure location, eats light food, and consumes in moderation— by these means, having restrained speech, body, and mind,
being thus controlled in speech, body, and thought, he is constantly and at all times intent upon that yoga which, through meditation, is the touch of Brahman.
Having again and again firmly relied upon detachment for the sake of ensuring the non-interruption of the [four] meditations. // 52 //

And then, regarding "egoism" (*ahaṃkāra*): having abandoned— meaning having specifically renounced through the power of yoga— egoism such as "I am detached," as well as forceful persistence, arrogance, and the characteristic of proceeding on a wrong path, along with desire, anger, and possessiveness even toward objects encountered due to the influence of *prārabdha-karma*, he remains free from attachment toward those things that have come upon him by force.

Being thus pacified and having attained supreme tranquility, he becomes fit and capable for the state of becoming Brahman—that is, for abiding with immovability in the realization "I am Brahman. //53//

Viśvanātha: Having restrained the self—the mind—by means of pure, *sāttvika* intellect and also by *sāttvika* fortitude, he is devoted to that supreme yoga which consists solely of meditation, that is, the contemplation of the Blessed One. "Strength" refers to being free from desire and passion, and not merely physical capability.
"Having liberated oneself from egoism and the like" means the cessation of ignorance.

"Peaceful," meaning possessing the tranquility of even the quality of *sattva*, refers to one who has performed the renunciation of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃnyāsa*). And as it is said: "One should renounce knowledge in Me" (BhP 11.19.1).
Thus, according to the statement in verse 11, the sense is that without the cessation of ignorance and knowledge, the experience of Brahman cannot arise.
It becomes fit—that is, capable—for "becoming Brahman," which is to say, for the experience of Brahman. (51–53)
Baladeva explains that method with the words "by means of the intellect" (buddhyā):

being endowed with a pure, sattvic intellect and having restrained the self—the mind—with such fortitude (dhṛti), one makes it fit for meditative absorption (samādhi). Having abandoned sense objects such as sound and having removed those [objects] from one's presence, one must also abandon passion and hatred, which are caused by them.

Having cast far away and abandoned [distractions], he dwells in solitude, staying in a secluded place; he eats light food, consuming in moderation; his speech and other faculties are restrained, directed toward the object of meditation;
and he is constantly devoted to the yoga of meditation, intent on contemplating Hari.
Dispassion (*vairāgya*) has as its object merely all things other than the self;
"I" refers to the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*),
which is the conceit that the body is the self.

Power (*bala*) is that which increases it, consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Arrogance (*darpa*) has that as its cause. Through the force of the remainder of past actions (*prārabdha-śeṣa*), when objects of enjoyment present themselves, there is desire (*kāma*), that is, longing;
and when they are seized by others, there is anger (*krodha*).
And possession has that [ego] as its object.

Therefore, having abandoned these—egoism and the rest—and being free from the sense of "mine," one becomes fit for becoming Brahman, which is to say, for attaining the nature of one's own self characterized by the eightfold qualities;
one experiences that.
He remains peaceful, like an ocean without waves. //51-53//
Established in Brahman, with a serene self, he neither grieves nor desires;
equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion unto Me. (18.54)
Śrīdhara: He states the fruit of abiding with unwavering steadiness in the thought "I am Brahman" with the words, "Brahman...

Having become Brahman, established in Brahman, and possessing a serene mind, he does not grieve for what is lost nor does he long for what is unattained, because of the absence of ego-identification with the body and so forth.

For this very reason, being equal toward all beings due to the absence of distraction caused by attachment, aversion, and the like, he attains supreme devotion characterized by the contemplation of Me in all beings. (54)
Viśvanātha: And then, upon the removal of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), having become Brahman, he is of the nature of Brahman by virtue of his unobscured consciousness; this is the meaning.
Because the impurity of the qualities has departed, he is both serene and the Self; thus he is "the Serene Self" (*prasannātmā*).
And thus, as in his previous state, he does not grieve for what is lost nor long for what is unattained, because of the absence of ego-identification with the body and so forth—this is the sense.
He is equal toward all beings, whether auspicious or inauspicious, like a child, because of the absence of external mental preoccupation—this is the sense.

Consequently, even when knowledge has become tranquil like a fire without fuel, he attains my imperishable devotion—which is inherent within that knowledge—in the form of hearing, chanting, and so on.

Because that [power] functions as my own essential nature (svarūpa-śakti) and is distinct from the power of illusion (māyā-śakti), it does not depart even when ignorance (avidyā) and its opposite (vidyā) have departed. For this very reason, it is "supreme" (parām)—meaning other than knowledge (jñāna) and superior to it—since it remains as the residue of desireless action (niṣkāma-karma), knowledge, and so forth; the sense is that it is "absolute" (kevalām). Regarding the phrase "he obtains": previously, although she existed as a subtle portion (kalā) for the sake of accomplishing liberation through knowledge, dispassion, and the like, there was no clear perception of her, as if she were the inner controller (antaryāmin) within all beings.
This is the intended meaning.

For this very reason, instead of saying "you should perform," the word "you shall obtain" (*labhate*) is employed. It is like the example: even when those who have gathered for the *māṣa-udgādi* offerings have perished, one obtains from them alone and separately, as if it were an indestructible golden casket.

However, since the attainment of complete *prema-bhakti* at that time is generally impossible, nor is its fruit *sāyujya*, it should therefore be explained that the word "supreme" (*parā*) refers to *bhakti* characterized by *prema*. //54//
Baladeva: He states the attainment that occurs subsequent to becoming Brahman with the words "Brahman...
One who has become Brahman is one who has directly realized his own essential nature endowed with the eightfold qualities.

"With a serene self" means being exceedingly pure due to the disappearance of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, its results (*vipāka*), and latent impressions (*āśaya*). In such expressions as "rivers with clear water," the meaning of the word *prasanna* is extreme purity.
Being thus constituted, he does not grieve for anyone other than Me, nor does he desire them;

he is equal toward all beings other than Me, whether high or low, regarding them as no different from a clod of earth or a piece of wood because they are equally fit to be abandoned. Being such as this, he attains supreme devotion to Me—that which is the culmination of knowledge, as stated in Gītā 18.50.
The meaning is that one attains the devotion described as characterized by my own experience, which possesses a form identical to the vision of me, and which is yet to be accomplished. //54//
By devotion one comes to know Me in truth—both who I am and what My extent is.
Then, having known Me in truth, one enters into Me immediately thereafter. 55.
Śrīdhara: And therefore, [the verse says] "by devotion.
Likewise, one comes to know Me in reality through supreme devotion.
In what manner?

The meaning is as follows: "I am that which is all-pervasive and the solid mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss (sac-cid-ānanda-ghana); having known Me truly in this way, immediately thereafter, upon the cessation of that knowledge, he enters Me, becoming one whose nature is supreme bliss. //55//

Viśvanātha: Now, one might ask: "What would happen to him at that time by means of that devotion which has been attained? To this, he says "by devotion" (*bhaktyā*), employing a shift in meaning (*arthāntaranyāsa*).

Whether he be a man of knowledge (*jñānī*) or a devotee of various kinds, he truly knows Me—whoever I am and of whatever nature I am—that very referent of the word "That" (*tat-padārtha*), solely through devotion.
For I have said: "I am to be grasped by exclusive devotion alone" (BhP 11.14.21).

Since this is so, therefore that aforementioned man of knowledge, immediately after that [state] through that very devotion, upon the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), at the subsequent time alone, having known Me, enters Me— he experiences the bliss of union with Me (*matsāyujya*). The sense is that because I transcend *māyā* and because ignorance is of the nature of *māyā*, I am understood even by means of knowledge (*vidyā*).

As for the statement in the *Nārada-pañcarātra* that "Sāṅkhya, Yoga, dispassion, austerity, and devotion to Keśava— this is the five-fold knowledge," and that devotion is heard of as a constituent of knowledge (*vidyā-vṛtti*),
that indeed is a certain portion of devotion itself— which is a function of the *hlādinī* potency— that has entered into knowledge for the sake of making knowledge fruitful.
For the sake of making one's actions fruitful, one enters even into the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*),
because it is stated that without that [devotion], the yogas of action, knowledge, and so forth are mere labor.
This is because devotion devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa-bhakti*) cannot, in reality, be a manifestation of knowledge (*vidyā*) which consists of the true qualities (*sad-guṇa*).

Therefore, the causality of knowledge (*vidyā*) consists solely in its function of removing ignorance; however, regarding the knowledge of the referent of that term [the Supreme], it is devotion alone that is the cause.
Furthermore, according to the Smṛti passage, "From *sattva* arises knowledge" (Gītā 14.17), knowledge born of *sattva* is indeed *sattva* itself.

And that *sattva* is expressed by the word "knowledge" (*vidyā*). Just so, knowledge arising from devotion is itself devotion; thus, it is sometimes called by the word "devotion" and sometimes by the word "knowledge.
Therefore, knowledge should also be understood as being of two kinds.

In this regard, one should understand—according to the perspective of the twenty-fifth chapter of the eleventh book—that having renounced the first kind of knowledge, one attains union with Brahman (*brahma-sāyujya*) through the second kind of knowledge.

In this regard, some, desiring union (*sāyujya*) through knowledge alone and devoid of devotion, are merely conceited knowers; their efforts bear fruit only in the form of suffering and are indeed highly censured.

Others, however, realizing that there is no liberation through knowledge alone without devotion, maintain that knowledge must be mixed with devotion. They consider the Lord’s body—which is composed of the *guṇas*—to be merely an adjunct of *māyā*, [and thus they seek] the stage of being established in yoga.
Even those who have attained [this state] are indeed wise, yet they are considered censurable because they pride themselves on being liberated. As it has been said:
"From the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet of Puruṣa, [the four castes] were born together with the stages of life (āśramas)."
The four social orders, beginning with the Brahmins, were born separately according to their qualities.
He who thus [knows] Puruṣa directly...
"They do not worship the Lord, who is the source of the self; having fallen from their station, they despise Him and fall downward. (BhP 11.5.3) Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: those who do not worship [Him], and even those who, though worshipping, treat Him with contempt—even if they are renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*)—fall downward, their knowledge being destroyed.
And so it has been said:
"Those others, O Lotus-eyed One, who consider themselves liberated..."
"Because their intellects are impure due to their lack of devotion toward You,
they ascend with great difficulty to the highest state, yet from there they fall back down, having disregarded Your feet. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.2.32) Thus it is said.
In this context, the word *āṅghri* (feet) is intentionally employed out of devotion alone.

The phrase "disregarding your feet" (*anādṛta-yuṣmad-aṅghrayaḥ*) refers specifically to the lack of regard for the body, based on the realization that the body is composed of qualities (*guṇa-maya*). As it has been said:
"The foolish disregard me."
"Having assumed a human body" (Gītā 9.11).
In reality, however, that human body is indeed *saccidānanda* (existence-consciousness-bliss);
its visibility, moreover, is due solely to the power of His grace, which is beyond the reach of fallacious reasoning.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇādhyātma*: "The Blessed One, though eternally unmanifest, is perceived through his own power."
"Without her, who could behold this Lord, the Supreme Bliss?

And thus, regarding the fact that the body of the Blessed One consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss, it is said: "He whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, seated beneath the celestial trees of Śrī Vṛndāvana. (GTU 1.33)

Even though there exist thousands of authoritative statements from Śruti and Smṛti, such as "assuming the body of Śabdabrahman," they nevertheless consider the Blessed Lord to have *māyā* as his limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) solely according to the perspective of the Śruti which says, "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10); however, He is endowed with His own essential, eternal power known as *māyā*.

Therefore, they do not accept the meaning of that scripture— cited as authoritative in the Mādhva commentary— which states, "Hence they declare the eternal Viṣṇu to be composed of *māyā*," because they hold that in the verse "But [the Lord projects] *māyā*," the word *māyā* refers exclusively to the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) which is identical with His own nature, and not to the power consisting of the three *guṇas* which is not identical with His nature.
Or rather, they do not even consider that one should know Maheśvara, Śambhu, as being of a difficult nature or as possessing the power of illusion (māyin).

Therefore, due to their offense against the Blessed One, even those who have attained the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukta) fall downward. As it is said in the *Pariśiṣṭa* passage cited in the *Vāsanābhāṣya*:
Even those liberated while living may again enter the latent tendencies of saṃsāra,
if [they do not rely] upon the inconceivable great power.
"O Blessed One, we are offenders.

Thinking thus, and considering that once the fruit has been attained there is no further need for the means (sādhana), they abandon both knowledge and even the devotion that was subordinate to it at the time of renouncing through knowledge;
yet, they falsely imagine themselves to have direct realization (aparokṣānubhava).
Due to the offense against the Śrī-vigraha, even those who possess devotion and knowledge lose it through its disappearance; they never again attain devotion.

Without devotion, they experience only the objects of that state as false meditations (mṛṣā-samādhayaḥ), and should be known as those who merely imagine themselves liberated while still living (jīvan-mukta-māninaḥ).
As it has been said: "O lotus-eyed one, those others who consider themselves liberated... [are such].

However, those who practice knowledge mixed with devotion, honoring the form of the Lord as consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who, upon the gradual cessation of ignorance and its opposite, attain supreme devotion—they are the liberated while living (jīvan-mukta). These are of two kinds:
some perform devotion for the sake of union (sāyujya), and having directly realized that state through that very devotion, they attain union within Him; these are indeed the "Saṅgītas."

Others, who are highly fortunate, by the power of associating with great devotees who are peaceful and spontaneous, abandon the desire for liberation and immerse themselves solely in tasting the sweetness of the nectar of devotion, like Śuka and others;
they indeed possess the highest association. As it is said:
"And the sages who delight in the Self..."
"Even the Nirgranthas, O Urukrama, practice causeless devotion; such are the qualities of Hari. (BhP 1.7.10) Thus [it is said].
Thus, in this way, the four types of knowers fall into two categories: those who are discordant [in their views] sink, while those who are harmonious cross over saṃsāra. //55//

Baladeva: To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "By devotion" (*bhaktyā*). By supreme devotion to Me—that is, by My bhakti—one truly knows and experiences Me, who I am in terms of My essential nature (*svarūpa*), My qualities (*guṇa*), and My manifestations (*vibhūti*). Then, because of that supreme devotion to Me, having known and experienced Me in truth according to My actual state (*yāthātmyena*), immediately thereafter, for that very reason, one enters Me; that is, one becomes united with Me.
In the phrase "he enters the city," only the conjunction with the city (*pura-saṃyoga*) is perceived, not the identity with the city itself (*purātmakatva*).
Here, it should be understood that devotion alone is stated to be the cause for both the true realization and the entry; as it is said:
"But by means of undivided devotion, [He] can be attained" (Gītā 11.54).
"Ādi" (and so forth) refers to what was stated previously.
"Immediately thereafter" means at a time subsequent to the authentic experience of My essential nature, qualities, and manifestations.
Alternatively, having known Me in truth through supreme devotion, he then enters Me by taking up that very devotion.
When a verbal root is elided, the fifth case is used for the object;
thus the author of the Sūtras says: "Even with respect to liberation, there is devotion, because it is seen in scripture that this [devotion] persists until death" (VS 4.1.12).
The meaning of the Sūtra is that from the time of death until liberation (*āprāyaṇād āmokṣāt*), devotion continues even with respect to that liberation, as it is observed in the Śruti.

The experts in the secret doctrine maintain that for those whose ignorance has been destroyed by devotion, the relish for devotion increases just as the taste of sugar increases for those whose bile has been cured by sugar.
Thus, the method of the means and the goal for those possessing steadfastness has been described. //55//
Even while constantly performing all actions, one who takes refuge in Me attains through My grace the eternal and imperishable state. 56.
Śrīdhara: With the words "all actions," he concludes the manner of liberation described as resulting from the propitiation of the Supreme Lord through one's own duties.

Performing all actions—both obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*)—at all times according to the sequence previously stated, one who has me as his refuge—that is, for whom I alone am the refuge to be sought and not the fruit such as heaven—attains the eternal [state] by my grace.
One attains the beginningless, supreme state. //56//

Viśvanātha: Thus, it has been stated that the man of knowledge (jñānī) attains union with Me (*mat-sāyujya*) through the renunciation of the fruits of action and the renunciation of action itself, respectively.
Now He says "sarva... to show how My devotee (*mad-bhakta*), moreover, attains Me.
"Mad-vyapāśrayaḥ" means one who takes refuge in Me specifically—even while still possessing desires; the sense is: "if even such a person [attains Me], how much more so a desireless devotee?"

The meaning is: even while performing all actions—whether obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or desire-driven (*kāmya*), as well as worldly activities characterized by the maintenance of sons, wife, and so forth—he is not a non-devotee; how much less so one who has abandoned the yoga of action, knowledge, and the worship of other deities, and is free from desire?
Here, by the prefix *ā-* in the phrase "he resorts to" (*āśrayate*) meaning "he serves properly," the act of service is shown to be the primary element.
By the word *api* ("also") in the phrase "even the ritual acts" (*karmāṇy api*), which indicates a degree of inferiority, it is shown that the ritual acts are subordinate.
Therefore, this person is one whose devotion is mixed with ritual action (*karma-miśra-bhaktimān*).
However, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to the karma described in the first hexad, which is characterized by being mixed with devotion (*bhakti*).
He attains the eternal, great station, my abode—Vaikuṇṭha, Mathurā, Dvārakā, Ayodhyā, and so forth.
Now, one might ask: how will those respective abodes remain during the great dissolution (*mahā-pralaya*)?
To this he replies: "Imperishable" means that even during the great dissolution (*mahā-pralaya*), nothing of My abode (*dhāman*) perishes because of My inconceivable power; this is the sense.

Now, it may be argued: surely the man of knowledge (*jñānī*) attains *sāyujya* (union) only when, through many births and many hardships such as austerities, there is complete cessation of all objects and senses, and only when there is freedom from action (*naiṣkarmya*).
How then can one attain Your eternal abode merely by taking refuge in You, even while remaining engaged in action and possessing desires?
Regarding that, he says "by my grace" (mat-prasādāt); the sense is: "Know that the power of my grace is indeed inconceivable. //56//
Baladeva: Now, with the two and a half verses beginning with "sarva," he speaks concerning those who are fully established.
One who takes refuge in Me and is exclusively devoted to Me performs all duties prescribed for himself as appropriate;
the word "api" (even) implies that although such a devotee is exclusively devoted to Me, there is no primary time [for ritual action] due to the absence of such time for him.
Thus says the author of the Sūtra: "In every way, because both characteristics are found there" (Vs 3.4.34).

By my grace, through my supreme favor, such a person attains—that is, obtains—the eternal, constant, immutable state known as the Supreme Ether, which consists of unchanging knowledge and bliss. //56//
Renouncing all actions with your mind in Me, regarding Me as the supreme goal, and taking refuge in the yoga of discernment, keep your mind constantly fixed on Me. 57.

Śrīdhara: Since this is so, therefore [it says] "with the mind. All actions—having renounced and surrendered them to Me with the mind, being *mat-paraḥ*, one for whom I alone am the supreme goal and the human aim to be attained.

Relying on yoga with a resolute intellect, even at the time of constantly performing actions, become one whose mind is fixed on Me alone, according to the principle stated in Gītā 4.24: "The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman... and so forth. 57.
Viśvanātha: Well then, what do you command me with certainty?
Am I to become a devotee without desire (*ananya-bhakta*), or am I indeed a devotee with desire (*sakāma-bhakta*) characterized by the features just mentioned?
In this regard, you will not be able to become one who is most excellent among all and devoted to no other,
nor will you be the least among all devotees; rather, become a devotee with desires—
this is what he means by saying "with the mind."
Having renounced—that is, having surrendered—all actions, including the duties of one's own stage of life (*svāśrama-dharma*) and worldly activities, unto Me;
"intent on Me" means one for whom I alone am the supreme goal and the human end to be attained; the meaning is that such a person is free from desire (*niṣkāma*).
As was stated previously:
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give,
and whatever austerity you practice, O Kaunteya—
"Therefore, perform that as an offering unto Me" (Gītā 9.27).
"Possessing the yoga of discernment through a resolute intellect, with your mind constantly fixed on Me—whether at the time of performing action or at other times—be one who remembers Me. (57)

Baladeva: Precisely because of that state, you, having surrendered all your own prescribed duties to Me, your Lord— with a mind free from the conceit of agency and the like— being intent on Me and regarding Me as your sole goal of life, take refuge in the yoga of the intellect and remain constantly with your mind fixed on Me at the time of performing those actions.

And this was already stated to you previously with the words "whatever you do" and so forth: perform actions only after having offered them [to Me], but not by performing them and then offering them afterwards. //57//
With your mind fixed on Me, you shall cross over all difficulties by My grace; but if, out of egoism, you will not listen to Me, you shall perish. 58.

Śrīdhara: Now, hear what will happen from that—“with mind fixed on Me” (*mac-citta*). Being with mind fixed on Me, by My grace you shall cross over all difficulties—that is, all the insurmountable sufferings of saṃsāra. He states the fault in the opposite case: “But if,” that is, if again, out of egoism—the conceit of being a knower—you do not listen to what has been spoken by Me, then you shall perish; you shall fall away from the goals of human life.
Viśvanātha: What follows from that? To this he says: "mac-citte" (in my mind) //58//
Baladeva: "Thus, with your mind fixed on Me, by My grace alone you shall cross over all difficulties and the insurmountable sufferings of saṃsāra;
do not worry about that.

As a friend to My devotees, I shall remove those [obstacles] and grant My very self. Thus has been stated the established method for those who have reached the goal regarding the path of means and the goal to be attained.

If, however, out of egoism—that is, the conceit of knowledge regarding what ought and ought not to be done—you do not listen to what I have said, then you shall perish; you will fall away from your own welfare.
For there exists no one other than Me who is the knower or the director of what ought and ought not to be done among living beings. (58)
If, relying on egoism, you think "I will not fight," this resolve of yours is vain; nature will compel you. (18.59)
Śrīdhara: If you think, "I shall perish at will, but I will not fight with my kinsmen," to that he says:
"That which is egoism...
Whatever resolve you form, thinking "I will not fight" while disregarding my words and relying solely on egoism—this determination of yours is indeed false, because of your lack of independence.
Regarding that, he says: "Nature, having transformed itself into the form of the quality of passion (rajas), will employ you; that is, it will set you in motion. //59//

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "But for me, a Kṣatriya, battle alone is the supreme duty; therefore, fearing the sin of killing my kinsmen, I do not wish to engage in it. To this, he says with a rebuke, "That which I...
*prakṛti* means one's own nature (*svabhāva*).

The sense is this: "Now you do not honor my words; however, when your natural enthusiasm for battle as a great hero arises and becomes irresistible, then, fighting yourself, you will laugh at me while slaying your own teachers such as Bhīṣma. //59//

Baladeva: Although for a Kṣatriya battle is indeed his duty, nevertheless, fearing the sin arising from the slaughter of my preceptor and Brahmins, I do not engage in it; if you think thus, "I will not fight," relying upon the ego—the conceit of knowing what ought and ought not to be done—then [you are mistaken].
In that case, this resolve and determination of yours will be false and fruitless;

for my nature, which is my *māyā* transformed through the quality of passion (*rajo-guṇa*), will surely impel you—who disregard my word—to engage in battle, using the slaughter of your elders and others as the pretext. 59.
Bound by your own karma born of your nature, O son of Kuntī, you shall do even against your will that which you do not wish to do because of delusion. (18.60)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "born of your own nature" (*svabhāvajena*):

*svabhāva* here refers to the cause of being a Kṣatriya, namely the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) from previous births. You are bound and constrained by your own duty—such as valor and so forth—as previously described; yet, out of delusion (*moha*), you do not wish to perform the action characterized by battle.
Even against your will, you shall certainly perform that action. //60//

Viśvanātha: He explains the very point already stated: "One's innate nature (*svabhāva*) is the cause of being a Kṣatriya; it is due to previous impressions (*pūrva-saṃskāra*). Therefore, one is bound and constrained by the action belonging to the class from which one was born. (60)
Baladeva: He establishes what has been said with the words "svabhāva" and so forth.

If, out of delusion—that is, through ignorance—you do not wish to engage in battle even as I have instructed you, then you will nonetheless perform it, bound helplessly by your own action born of your nature (svabhāva), namely your valor, which is manifested by my Māyā. //60//
The Lord dwells, O Arjuna, in the heart-region of all beings,
causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion, as if they were mounted on a machine.

Śrīdhara: Thus, with these two verses, the dependence on *prakṛti* and the dependence on inherent nature (*svabhāva*) according to the systems of Sāṅkhya and others have been stated. Now, he states his own view with the two verses beginning with "The Lord" (*īśvara*).
The Lord, as the inner controller (*antaryāmī*), dwells in the center of the hearts of all beings.
Doing what? Causing all beings to wander by means of his own power, *māyā*, setting them into their respective actions;
the meaning is that it is just as a puppeteer in the world causes artificial beings mounted on wooden machines to move about.
Or rather, the meaning is that he causes the beings who have mounted the "machines"—that is, the bodies—to wander, namely the individual souls (*jīvas*) who identify with the body.
And likewise, there is a mantra of the Śvetāśvataras:
"The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings."
"The overseer of karma, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious one, absolute and devoid of qualities" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11).

And also the Antaryāmi-Brāhmaṇa: "He who, dwelling within the self, controls the self from within, whom the self does not know, whose body the self is—he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal."
And so forth. //61//
Viśvanātha: Having stated the view of the proponents of [inherent] nature (svabhāvavādins) with two verses, he states his own position: "The Lord is Nārāyaṇa, the inner controller of all;
He who, dwelling in the earth, is within the earth, whom the earth does not know."
"He whose body is the earth,
who controls the earth from within" (BAU 3.6.3);
and whatever else there is in this world—
Whether it is seen or even heard,
Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all of that, both within and without.
The Lord who is the inner controller, as established by such scriptural passages as the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad (13.5), dwells in the heart.
What is he doing? [He is] all...

The meaning is as follows: by means of His own power, *māyā*, He causes all beings to wander and revolve, setting them in motion toward their respective actions; just as *māyā* causes artificial dolls mounted on a mechanical device—such as one operated by the movement of a string—to move about, so too does She cause all beings to be deluded.
Alternatively, the meaning is that She causes all individual souls (*jīvas*) who are mounted upon a machine—that is, mounted upon a body—to wander. //61//

Baladeva: Observing that Arjuna still harbors the conceit of being a knower, the Lord instructs him through two verses on the basis that [the Self] cannot be abandoned because it is the very essence of consciousness. "O Arjuna, if you consider yourself a knower, then [you must know] that Lord whom you have come to know from the *Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa*, who dwells in the heart-region of all beings—from Brahmā down to the stationary objects—and who, by means of His own power, *māyā*, causes them to revolve."

"It causes all beings to enter the machine" means that they have mounted the machine—which is fashioned by *māyā* and characterized by the body, senses, and vital breaths—in accordance with their karma.
This is illustrated by a metaphor: just as a puppeteer makes artificial beings mounted on wooden machines move about, so it is here. //61//
Go to Him alone for refuge with your whole being, O Bharata; by His grace you shall attain supreme peace and the eternal abode. 62.
Śrīdhara: Regarding the word "him" (*tam*):

since all living beings are thus dependent upon the Supreme Lord, therefore, having abandoned egoism, take refuge in that Lord alone with your whole being and entire self. And from His grace alone, you shall attain supreme, ultimate peace and the eternal, perpetual abode of the Supreme Lord. //62//

Viśvanātha: He states the purpose of making this known with the words "that very [state]," etc. "That" refers to the cessation of both higher and lower ignorance; and from that, the eternal abode, Vaikuṇṭha.

Some say that this is the taking of refuge in the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), which pertains only to those who worship the Inner Controller; whereas for those who worship the Blessed Lord, there is the taking of refuge in the Blessed Lord, which will indeed be explained further on.
"But as for that other one who is my chosen deity, Śrī Kṛṣṇa—he alone is my guru; he instructs me with teachings that are favorable and beneficial for the yoga of devotion.
Meditate constantly, thinking: 'I take refuge in him.
As it was said by Uddhava:
O Lord, the sages, their joy increased as they remember the deeds performed even by those whose life is dedicated to sacred knowledge (*brahmayus*), do not find sufficient honor for You—
You who, from within and without, shake off the impurity of embodied beings.
"Through the form of the preceptor and the shrine, he reveals his own state. (BhP 11.29.6) //62//
Baladeva: Then, take refuge in that very Lord with your whole being—that is, through the activity of your body and other faculties.
If it is asked, "What follows from that?", he says:
"That [peace]"—namely, supreme peace, characterized by the complete separation from all afflictions.
You shall attain that abode which is eternal, constant, and stable, and which is celebrated in the Vedas as "that supreme state of Viṣṇu" and so forth.
And He is the Lord, who am indeed your friend, and I am seated in the heart of all— thus [it is said in Gītā 15.15].

Furthermore, because you yourself have accepted [the Supreme] through such statements as "The Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Abode" (Gītā 10.12), following my own previous declarations which seek the consensus of the celestial sages and others;
and because [it] has been directly perceived in the vision of the Universal Form.
Therefore, remain steadfast in my instruction. //62//
Thus has this knowledge, more secret than all secrets, been declared to you by Me. Having reflected upon it in its entirety, do as you wish. (18.63)
Śrīdhara: Concluding the entire meaning of the Gītā, he says "iti" (thus).

In this manner (*ity anena prakāreṇa*), that knowledge (*jñāna*) has been declared (*ākhyāta*) and taught (*upadiṣṭa*) to you (*te*) by me, who am omniscient (*sarvajña*) and supremely compassionate (*parama-kāruṇika*).
Of what nature is it?

This Gītā-śāstra, which I have taught, is more secret than even the most secret knowledge, such as the yoga of secret mantras; having reflected upon it in its entirety, do thereafter as you wish. The sense is that once this has been reflected upon, your delusion will cease. //63//

Viśvanātha: He concludes the entire meaning of the Gītā with the words "iti" (thus). Knowledge—meaning that by which [reality] is known—is the science of knowledge (*jñāna-śāstra*) concerning Karma-yoga, Aṣṭāṅga-yoga, and Jñāna-yoga;
it is "more secret than the secret" because of its extreme esoteric nature, such that it has not been [fully disclosed] even by Vasiṣṭha, Bādarāyaṇa, Nārada, and others.

Alternatively, [the meaning is]: "That which has not been revealed in their own respective treatises"—or rather, because their omniscience is relative while mine is absolute, they do not know this due to its extreme secrecy;
and for the very same reason of extreme secrecy, I have not taught this to them in any way whatsoever—this is the intended sense.
Having reflected upon this entirely and without exception,
act in whatever manner you desire and in whatever way you wish to do it.
Thus the final hexad of knowledge is complete.
This entire scripture of the Śrī Gītā, the crest-jewel of all sciences, consists of three hexads; it is a most precious and profound casket of devotion.
The first hexad of action serves as its golden base and lid.
It is thus: the final group of six verses has a golden upper cover inlaid with jewels.

Between those two, the devotion residing in the middle group of six shines as a supreme great jewel that captivates Śrī Kṛṣṇa and is priceless in the three worlds; its attendant is understood to be the pair of pure verses consisting of sixty-four syllables beginning with "man-manā bhava," which occupy half of that upper cover. //63//
Baladeva: Concluding the scripture, he says "iti" (thus).
This knowledge, characterized by the modes previously described, is the Gītā-śāstra—so called according to its etymology (*nirukti*) as that by which action, devotion, and knowledge are known.
That, consisting of such [knowledge], has been narrated (*ākhyātam*) and fully proclaimed (*samproktam*) to you by me.
"More secret than the secret"—meaning more hidden than the scriptures concerning secret mantras and the like—it is to be guarded.
Having reflected upon this entire scripture in its entirety, you may thereafter do as you wish.
Once this has been thoroughly considered, the destruction of your delusion and your steadfastness in my words will come to pass. //63//
Listen again to my supreme word, the most secret of all secrets.
Since you are dearly beloved to Me, I shall therefore speak what is for your benefit.

Śrīdhara: Out of compassion for one who is unable to fully contemplate the extremely profound Gītā-śāstra, [the Lord] Himself summarizes its essence and speaks in three verses beginning with "The most secret of all secrets.
Listen to My words, which are the most secret of all secrets—even though they have been spoken here and there—now being spoken again.

He states the reason for speaking again and again: "Thinking that you are *dṛḍham*—that is, extremely (*atyantam*)—dear (*iṣṭaḥ*) and beloved (*priyaḥ*) to me (*me*), for that very reason I shall speak what is for your benefit.

Alternatively, the meaning is: "Having ascertained that you are dear to me and that what I am about to say is *dṛḍham*—that is, endowed with all means of valid knowledge—I shall therefore speak it to you.
Some read the word as *dṛḍha-matiḥ*. //64//

Viśvanātha: Then, perceiving his dear friend Arjuna—who had remained silent while attempting to contemplate the *Gītā-śāstra* of exceedingly profound meaning—the Blessed One, whose heart was like fresh butter melted with compassion, said: "O dear friend Arjuna, I myself shall proclaim the essence of all scriptures in eight verses."
"Enough of your distress from deliberating on this and that," he says with the word "all" (*sarva*).
The word "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*) refers to what was previously stated at the end of the chapter on the Royal Science and the Royal Secret:
"Be intent on Me, be My devotee..."
"Offer sacrifice to Me, bow down to Me;
thus, with your self disciplined and having Me as your supreme goal, you shall come to Me alone. (Gītā 9.34)

That which is indeed the supreme essence of the meaning of all scriptures, and the very essence even of the Gītā scripture, is the most secret; there is nothing more secret than this anywhere, from anyone, or in any way—this is the sense, namely that it is indivisible.
He states the reason for speaking again:

"You are highly esteemed by me; you are exceedingly dear to me, for you are my friend. For that very reason, [the Lord says], "I have your welfare at heart"; the sense is that one should not speak of anything whatsoever—even that which is not a great secret—to anyone who is not a friend. There is also a reading: *dṛḍhamatiḥ* (of firm intellect). //64//
Baladeva: Now, intending to teach the method of means and ends for those who are independent [of other paths], He first praises that method with the words "all" (*sarva*).
"The greatest secret" (*sarva-guhyatamam*) means the secret that excels among all secrets.
