By the word "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*), He indicates that although this was previously taught in the chapter on the Royal Science (*rāja-vidyā*) through such statements as "Fix your mind on Me" (*man-manā bhava*), it is being stated again at the end because of its extreme dearness to Him; listen to this supreme [teaching], which is the very essence of the entire Gītā scripture.
This is the essential point. Furthermore, by saying "you are my cause," it means you are my beloved,
my most cherished one.

Since you have ascertained that my word is firm and endowed with all means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), I shall speak what is for your benefit; nevertheless, the sense is that this alone must be practiced. (64) BhG 18.65
Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me;
thus you shall come to Me alone—this I promise you in truth, for you are dear to Me. 65.
Śrīdhara: Thus he said, "Fix your mind on Me" (*man-manāḥ*). Be one whose mind is fixed on Me; be My devotee, characterized by the habit of worshiping Me.
Sacrifice to Me—be one whose nature is to worship Me—and bow down to Me alone. Acting in this way, you shall come to Me, that is, attain Me, through the knowledge obtained by My grace;
do not entertain any doubt in this matter.
For you are indeed dear to me; therefore, so that it may be true, I promise and make a vow to you. //65//
Viśvanātha: "Be one whose mind is fixed on Me" (man-manā bhava) means that you should contemplate Me precisely as My devotee;

the sense is not that you should perform meditation on Me by becoming a knower (jñānī) or a yogi. Alternatively, "be one whose mind is fixed on Me" means [meditate] upon Me, Śyāmasundara, whose hair is beautifully glossy and curled, and whose moon-like face rains down the nectar of sweet glances of compassion from its beautiful creeper-like eyebrows.
Become one whose mind you offer as a gift;
or rather, He says, "Become My devotee"—

that is, worship Me by means of all the senses through hearing, chanting, beholding My form, sweeping and smearing My temple, gathering flowers for Me, and offering My garlands, ornaments, parasols, chowries, and so forth.
"Perform [it], or else give me perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings; thus he says: 'Become my sacrificer;
perform my worship.'"
Alternatively, he says, "Give me even a mere salutation; bow down to me by prostrating on the ground, or perform the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma).
Perform either the combination of these four—contemplation of me, service, worship, and prostration—or any one of them."
"You shall come to Me; you shall attain Me. Offer your mind, offer your ears and other senses, or offer fragrances, flowers, and so forth.
It is the truth that I shall give My very Self to you—this is for you alone."
The sense is: "Do not have any doubt in this matter.

Amara states: *satyam* is used for both an oath and truth. Now, one might object that the people born in the land of Mathurā swear an oath at every word; [the author replies: "Truly, I promise"—that is, having made a solemn vow, I speak.
The underlying meaning is: "You are dear to me; for no one who is dear would ever deceive another. //65//
Baladeva said: He spoke these words, "Be one whose mind is fixed on Me.

This has been explained previously: by virtue of having the mind fixed on Me, you shall reach Me alone—Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, who possesses qualities such as being dark-complexioned like a blue lotus, who is exceedingly dear to you, and who has manifested in human form. You shall attain Him alone.

The meaning is this: it is not my other form characterized by a thousand heads and so forth, nor the thumb-sized inner controller (antaryāmin), nor forms such as Nṛsiṃha or Varāha that I shall give; rather, I shall give you my very self as your friend. "To you, I shall give my own self as your companion"—this is your true oath (*satyaṃ śapathaḥ*). According to the *Nānārthavarga*, "truth" (*satya*) and "oath" (*śapatha*) are synonymous.
The intention here is: "Do not have any doubt in this matter."
[The opponent objects: "But surely, because you are a native of Mathurā, even by taking an oath there would be no destruction of my doubt. To this he replies: "I promise"—having made a vow, I said:
"Because you are dear to me; for natives of Mathurā do not deceive one who is dear to them with a friendly heart.
What then to speak of one who is most beloved? Such is the sense.
He for whom I have great affection has likewise [affection] for me;
as I have already stated in the passage beginning with "For he is dear to me," I am unable to endure separation from him.
Therefore, place your trust in my words; you shall indeed attain Me. //65//
Abandoning all duties, take refuge in Me alone. I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve. (18.66)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, he speaks of that which is most secret with the words "all" (*sarva*):
"By devotion to Me alone—through firm conviction that everything will come to pass—abandon ritual service (*vidhi-kaiṅkarya*) and take refuge in Me alone.
Do not grieve, thinking that by acting thus there might be sin resulting from the abandonment of prescribed duties; do not fear liberation."
Since you have me as your sole refuge, I shall liberate you from all sins. //66//

Viśvanātha: Now, one might ask: "Is that meditation and so forth which I perform to be preceded by the performance of the duties of my own stage of life (*āśrama*), or is it to be done alone? To this he replies: "Having abandoned all duties—that is, all the duties of the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*)—take refuge in Me alone.

It should not be explained as "having abandoned" meaning "having renounced [the world]," because Arjuna, being a Kṣatriya, lacks the qualification for formal renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). Nor did the Blessed Lord, addressing Arjuna, give this instruction solely to a group of other people.
Thus it should be stated:

since it is appropriate to apply the instruction toward Arjuna, who is the actual subject of the teaching, it is possible that others might also be instructed; however, this is not the case otherwise.

Furthermore, the phrase "without abandoning" (*na ca parityajya*) must be explained as having its purport solely on the renunciation of the fruits [of action]. This is how this statement is to be interpreted.
O King, he who has with his whole being taken refuge in the Refuge-worthy is neither a servant nor a debtor to the gods, sages, spirits, humans, or ancestors.
Having abandoned all ritual acts, when a mortal has offered himself and desires to act for my sake, he goes to Mukunda, leaving behind his [worldly] duties. (BhP 11.5.41)
Then, attaining immortality,
he indeed becomes fit for identity with Me;
until then, one should perform ritual actions.
One should not become weary until such time as faith arises toward hearing my stories and other such practices. (BhP 11.20.9)
He who, having fully understood both virtues and faults—
even those pertaining to himself that were enjoined by me— renounces all dharmas;
For it must necessarily be explained that these words of the Blessed One, such as "he shall worship me, O best of beings" (BhP 11.11.37), share the same meaning [as the previous statement],
and because the word *pari-* is employed here.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Take refuge in Me alone, and not in dharma, knowledge, yoga, other deities, and so forth.

For previously, since you did not have the qualification for devotion to anyone other than Me—which is the most excellent—therefore, by My speaking such words as "Whatever you do, whatever you eat," and so on, [I directed you] toward devotion mixed with action (karma-miśrā bhakti).
Your qualification has been stated.

Now, however, out of extreme compassion, she has granted you the qualification for exclusive devotion (ananya-bhakti) itself; the sense is that she has set aside even her own established rule—namely, that such exclusive devotion is obtainable only through her grace toward those who are exclusively devoted to her by chance—just as she set aside her vow during the battle with Bhīṣma.
Furthermore, no apprehension of sin can arise for you regarding the abandonment of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites by my command.

Since the performance of obligatory rites was previously enjoined by me alone in the form of the Vedas, whereas now their abandonment is enjoined in its very essence, how could sins possibly accrue to you from the non-performance of obligatory rites?

On the contrary, it should be understood that from this point forward, sins will accrue even from the performance of obligatory duties (*nitya-karman*), because of the direct transgression of My command.
Indeed, whoever takes refuge in someone becomes dependent upon them like a purchased animal.
Whatever he causes him to do, that very thing he does;
wherever he places him, right there he stands.
"That which one causes others to eat,
that very thing one eats oneself"— this is the reality of the dharma characterized by taking refuge.
As it is stated in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*:
The resolve for conformity, the avoidance of opposition,
the conviction that [the Lord] will protect, the choosing of Him as protector, the entrusting of oneself, and freedom from despondency— this is the sixfold refuge. Thus it is said.

"Conformity" (*ānukūlya*) is activity directed toward one's chosen deity as enjoined by the scriptures of devotion, which is pleasing to that deity; "non-conformity" (*prātikūlya*) is the opposite of that.
Regarding "in His capacity as protector": it is the conviction that He alone is one's protector and no other.

Regarding "He will protect": it is the confidence—like that of Draupadī, the lordly elephant, and others—that even when circumstances unfavorable to one's own protection arise, He will certainly protect one.

"Surrender" (niḥkṣepana) is the dedication of oneself, together with one's own gross and subtle bodies, solely for the sake of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. "Absence of wretchedness" (akārpaṇya) is the refusal to manifest one's own misery anywhere else. That state of taking refuge is one in which these six matters are practiced according to the instructions of the Creator.
Therefore, from this day forward, if I am indeed one who has gone to you for refuge, then whatever may happen—whether auspicious or inauspicious—that alone must be my duty.
In that regard, if you cause me to perform only what is righteous (*dharma*), then there is no concern at all.

But if, by virtue of your sovereignty, you act according to your own whims and cause me to perform only what is unrighteous (*adharma*), then what will be my fate? To this he says: "I... [and so forth].
I shall liberate you from all sins—whatever have existed in the past and the present, and whatever I myself shall cause to be committed;
the sense is that I am not like another refuge who is incapable in that regard. Relying solely upon you, I have taught this scripture merely for the sake of the world.
"Do not grieve; do not feel sorrow for your own sake or for the sake of others.

Let everyone in the world, including yourself and others, abandon all duties pertaining to self and others, and instead, intent upon meditation on Me and so forth, take refuge in Me and live in happiness.
The burden of liberating them from sin and even the burden of liberating them from saṃsāra have already been accepted by Me."
For those people who, thinking of no other, worship me with constant devotion; for them who are ever-exerting themselves—
"I carry their well-being" (Gītā 9.22).

"Alas! I have placed such a burden upon my own Master"—do not feel grief even for this, for there is not even a trace of effort on the part of Me, who am affectionate toward My devotees. Since there is nothing further to be taught beyond this, the scripture is brought to its conclusion. //66//

Baladeva: [Objection: "But how can your pure devotion—consisting of worship, prostration, and so forth—be performed by a person whose heart is stained by infinite sins in the form of past karma, as long as those infinite sins, which are opposed to devotion to You, have not been destroyed by prescribed rites such as *kṛcchra* penances and other religious duties? To this, He says: "All... (sarva...).

Having abandoned all prescribed duties such as the *kṛcchra* penances which serve as expiation for past sins— having relinquished them in their very nature— and having taken refuge in Me, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of All, who has manifested in many forms such as Nṛsiṃha and Dāśarathi (Rāma),
who am the object of pure devotion, the singular destroyer of all desires including ignorance;
But do not go for refuge to anyone other than Me, such as Śitikaṇṭha (Śiva) and others; rather, take refuge in Me alone.

I am the worthy refuge, the Lord of all, and I shall liberate you—who have come to Me for refuge—from all sins, that is, from the effects of your past actions. Thus, a mutual duty has been shown. Do not grieve.

The meaning is: "Do not grieve, thinking, 'How can those difficult practices such as the Kṛcchra penances—which require a very long time to accomplish—be performed by me, who have a short lifespan and desire purity of heart?
For it has been stated here that these [difficulties] shall not exist for one who takes refuge in Me."
And the Śruti says thus: "Neither by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality";
and likewise, "He realizes [the Self] through the yoga of faith, devotion, and meditation," and so forth.
These duties are to be performed respectively for the purification of the hearts of those established in their vows, and for the welfare of the world by those who are fully perfected.
This is understood from such scriptural passages as "Him [the Self]... and "By truth this Self is to be attained, indeed by austerity...
Furthermore, one should not grieve, thinking that by abandoning what is enjoined one would incur sin characterized as transgression;

for while there might be such a consequence for a renunciant (yati) who abandons the Agnihotra and other rites by the command of the Veda, it is impossible for the seeker of refuge to incur such a fault by abandoning those same rites by the command of the Supreme Lord.
On the contrary, there would be the incurrence of fault in transgressing that instruction;
nor, because of the incurrence of sin from abandoning what is enjoined by its very nature,
should it be explained as "all [these] are the fruits of dharma."
Because there would be no transgression in the case of abandoning the fruit [of action].
Therefore, for one who has surrendered, there is an abandonment of duty in its essential nature.

Nor does it follow that he must perform his own specific duties by the logic of "for nowhere indeed... and so forth; because for one who is devoted to worshipping Him and the like, there is no such obligation according to that same logic.

And thus, just as for one established in the [lower] path there is conduct according to dharma ending in the experience of the self, and for one established in the ultimate there is it ending in the experience of the supreme Self, so too for the seeker (prapattṛ) there is purity of the inner self; this has been stated precisely in the Eleventh [Book]: "One should perform ritual actions until one becomes weary [of them]."
"Or until faith arises from hearing my stories and so forth.
This is called taking refuge (*śaraṇāgati*), which is *prapatti* consisting of six limbs.
The resolve for conformity, the avoidance of opposition,
the conviction that [He] will protect, the choosing [Him] as protector,
and the surrender of oneself in humility— this is the sixfold taking of refuge.
Thus it is stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"Conformity" is activity that is pleasing to Hari and is prescribed by the scriptures of devotion;
its opposite, however, is "contrariety."
"Entrusting oneself" (ātma-nikṣepaḥ) means placing one's own burden upon that refuge.
"Wretchedness" (kārpaṇyam) means being subject to friction or distress.
In some readings, the text states: "entrusting [oneself] is not wretchedness" (nikṣepaṇam akārpaṇyam).
In that context, "miserliness" (kārpaṇya) is the manifestation of one's own wretchedness toward another;
the rest is clear. 66.
This should never be spoken by you to one who lacks austerity, nor to one who is not devoted, nor to one who does not wish to listen, nor to one who finds fault with Me.
Śrīdhara: Having thus taught the essential truth of the meaning of the Gītā, he states the rule for its propagation with the words "this":
this essential truth of the Gītā's meaning must not be spoken by you (*te*) to one who lacks austerity (*atapaskāya*), that is, to one devoid of the performance of dharma;

nor should it ever be spoken to one who is not a devotee (*abhaktāya*), that is, to one void of devotion toward the guru and the Lord; nor should it be spoken to one who does not desire to hear (*aśuśrūṣave*), that is, to one who does not perform service.
To one who shows malice toward Me, the Supreme Lord—meaning one who reviles Me by attributing faults through a human perspective—to him this should not be spoken. //67//
Viśvanātha: Having thus instructed the scripture of the Gītā, he states the rule for the propagation of the tradition with the words "this" and so forth.
It must not be told to one who lacks austerity—that is, to one whose senses are not restrained—since the Smṛti declares: "The one-pointedness of the mind and the senses is the highest austerity.
Even if the senses are restrained, it must not be told to one who is not a devotee.

Even though I possess the three attributes such as self-restraint of the senses, I shall by no means speak to him who bears malice toward me—that is, who imputes the fault of being identical with Māyā to me, the Supreme Brahman free from all limiting conditions. //67//
Baladeva: Now, He teaches that this Gītā scripture, which He Himself has taught, is to be given only to worthy recipients and not to unworthy ones, with the words "This...
This scripture must not be spoken by you to one who lacks austerity (*atapaska*), nor to one whose senses are unsubdued.

Even if he possesses austerity, it must not be spoken to one who lacks devotion—that is, one who is devoid of devotion to You, the teacher of the scripture, and to Me, the subject of the scripture, the Lord of All.
It should not be spoken even to an ascetic who is devoted but does not serve or does not wish to hear;

nor indeed should it be spoken to one who is envious of me—the Lord of all, whose form consists of eternal qualities—by attributing to me a form composed of illusory qualities. For this reason, he is designated with a distinct grammatical case.
Thus the author of the Sūtra says: "Not manifesting [the gender], because of the concordance" (Pāṇini 3.4.50). //67//
He who shall declare this supreme secret among My devotees,
having offered supreme devotion to Me, will undoubtedly come to Me alone. (18.68)
Śrīdhara: By the word "yaḥ" (he who), he states the fruit for one who teaches the scripture of the Gītā when it is free from these defects:
"He will speak among my devotees" means he will speak to my devotees;
"he performs supreme devotion unto me" means that, being thereby freed from doubt, he attains me alone—this is the meaning. //68//
Viśvanātha: With the two verses beginning with "yaḥ," he states the fruit for the teacher.
By the phrase "having performed supreme devotion," first there is the attainment of supreme devotion, and from that, the attainment of Me.
This pertains to the teacher. //68//

Baladeva: He states the fruit for the teacher of the scripture with the words "yaḥ" (he who). For such a teacher, first there is the attainment of devotion to Me as the Supreme, and from that, the attainment of My own abode follows. //68//
And among men, there is none who performs what is more pleasing to Me than he;
nor shall there be anyone else on earth more dear to Me than he.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the words "nor indeed" (*na ceti*):
therefore, among men, there is no one other than My devotees who explains the Gītā scripture who is *priyakṛttamaḥ*—that is, one who causes Me extreme satisfaction.
Nor will there be anyone else than them in the future; even for Me, at present, there is none on earth more dear than they.
And the meaning is that it will not come to pass even at another time. //69//
Viśvanātha: Therefore, there is no one other than the teacher who is more affectionate or more beloved. //69//
Baladeva: "Not so.

Therefore, among men, there has never been before, nor will there ever be, anyone other than the teacher of the Gītā who performs for me that which is most dear—that is, who brings me such supreme satisfaction.
On this earth, there has never been anyone more beloved to me than he, nor will there ever be. //69//
And whoever shall study this sacred dialogue of ours, by him I shall have been worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge; such is my conviction. (18.70)
Śrīdhara: He states the fruit for one who recites it with the words "He who shall study" (*adhyeṣyate*).
"He who shall study"—meaning he who will recite in the form of a *japa*—this dialogue between us, Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, which is righteous (*dharmyam*), that is, not departing from dharma;
by that person I would be worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge (*jñāna-yajña*), which is superior to all sacrifices. This is my conviction.
Even if he recites [the mantra] merely by rote, without understanding the meaning of the *Gītā*, nevertheless, as I listen to it, the thought arises in me: "He is revealing me.
Just as in the world, when someone happens to utter another's name at some time or place, that person approaches them thinking, "This person is calling for me."
In the same way, may I also be present for him.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Just as I was pleased with Ajāmila, Kṣatrabandhu, and others merely by their uttering my name in some manner, so too shall I be pleased with this one. //70//
Viśvanātha: He states the fruit of this study [in the verse beginning] "adhyeṣyate" (it will be studied). //70//
Baladeva: Now, he states the fruit for the student of the scripture with the words, "And he shall study.

Here, the meaning is that because I am of the opinion that I would be pleased and honored merely by the recitation of this [text]—that sacrifice of knowledge which has been described there—I am easily attained by him.
Even that man who, full of faith and free from malice, should merely hear this,
he too, being liberated, shall attain the auspicious worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds. (18.71)

Śrīdhara: He states that there is a fruit even for someone other than the one reciting who hears [it], beginning with the words "one who has faith" (*śraddhāvān*). This refers to a person endowed with faith who merely listens; furthermore, it is said in order to exclude the fault of anyone who, though possessing faith, perceives defects such as asking, "For what purpose does he recite so loudly? or "Is he reciting incoherently? (*abaddha*)? To counteract that, he says:
And he who listens without envy—that is, free from malice—shall also be liberated from all sins and attain the worlds of those who have performed meritorious deeds such as the horse sacrifice. //71//
Viśvanātha: He states the fruit of hearing this [text] with the words "one who possesses faith" (śraddhāvān) //71//
Baladeva: He states the fruit for the listener with the words "śraddhayā" (with faith).

Even he who merely listens with faith, being free from envy—meaning not perceiving faults such as "Why is this being recited loudly? or "Why is it impure?"—he too, liberated from all sins, shall attain the worlds of those of meritorious deeds who perform sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha.
Or else, [he leads them] to the worlds of those who possess merit and devotion, such as the Dhruvaloka and other varieties of Vaikuṇṭha; this is the meaning. //71//
"O Pārtha, has this been heard by you with a one-pointed mind? O Dhanañjaya, has the delusion born of ignorance been destroyed in you? (18.72)
Śrīdhara: With the intention that he might instruct him again should perfect understanding fail to arise, he says, "Kaccit" (I hope). "Kaccit" has the sense of a question.
"Ajñāna-sammoha" is the delusion of ignorance, a misconception produced by the lack of knowledge of reality.
The rest is clear. //72//
Viśvanātha: With the intention that "I shall instruct again once correct understanding has been established," he says, "Kaccit" (Is it so?). //72//
Baladeva: Thus, the scripture and the greatness of its recitation and so forth have been described.
Now, he asks "kaccit" regarding the comprehension of the meaning of the scripture and the experience thereof;
here, "kaccit" is an indeclinable used in the sense of inquiry.
The intention is that he will teach this again once the correct realization has not yet arisen. //72//
Arjuna said:
Delusion has been destroyed and memory regained by me through your grace, O Acyuta.
I stand firm, my doubts dispelled; I shall carry out your word.
Śrīdhara: Having attained his purpose, Arjuna said, "It is destroyed.
Delusion regarding the Self has been destroyed, because by Your grace I have regained my memory, which consists of the contemplation of my true nature as "I am this [Self].
Therefore, I stand firm; I have risen for battle.
"I, whose doubt regarding the domain of Dharma has vanished, shall carry out your command. //73//
Viśvanātha: What more than this shall I ask? He says, "I have abandoned all duties and have come to You for refuge; I am free from anxiety, trusting in You alone.
By saying "lost" and "I shall do," he means that henceforth, remaining under the command of You, my refuge, is the sole duty of me who has sought refuge.
It is not the duty of his own stage of life (*āśrama-dharma*), nor is there any regard for the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*).

"But from this day forward, you must indeed abandon them. Then the Blessed One said, "O dear friend Arjuna, there remains a certain task for me to perform in removing the burden of the earth; I desire to accomplish that through you alone. When this was said, Arjuna, with the Gāṇḍīva bow in hand, rose up to fight. //73//

Baladeva: Thus questioned, Pārtha spoke of his scriptural experience and realization by way of its fruit, saying "It is destroyed. Delusion—characterized by erroneous knowledge—has been destroyed by your grace alone; and memory, which consists in being fixed upon things as they truly are, has been regained by me. I am now free from doubt, with my uncertainty severed, and I stand firm.
"I shall do as you say.

This is what is meant: all living beings, including gods, humans, and others, are independent in their respective actions; they possess pride in their bodies and honor the gods who are themselves honored by men and who grant them their desires.
But who is this so-called "Lord" (Īśvara)? What kind of being is he?

Indeed, that delusion which previously existed in me— characterized by the erroneous cognition that He is devoid of qualities, formless, and indifferent, while *prakṛti* is the cause of the universe— that has been destroyed through the instruction obtained from You. [For You are] the Lord of all, the friend of devotees, whose essential nature is endowed with the power called *parā*, whose form is consciousness and bliss, and who is a mine of jewels of attributes such as omniscience, omnipotence, and the realization of true resolves.

By His mere will, through the powers known as *prakṛti*, *jīva*, and *kāla*, He effects the manifold creation in accordance with the karma of living beings; He bestows everything up to Himself upon His devotees, yet His own wealth consists solely of those who possess nothing.
You are that very one, my friend, the son of Vasudeva—such was my realization of the ultimate truth.
Therefore, I have now taken refuge in you and remain here.
My doubt—that you might ever abandon me—has also been severed.

Now, if the removal of the earth’s burden is your own purpose, then I shall carry out those words of yours, since I am one who has taken refuge [in you]. Thus spoke Arjuna, rising with bow in hand. (73)
Saṃjaya said:
Thus have I [related] the conversation of Vāsudeva and the high-souled Pārtha.
I heard this wonderful conversation, which causes the hair to stand on end.
Śrīdhara: Thus, having related the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna to Dhṛtarāṣṭra and resuming the narrative at hand, Sañjaya said: "Thus...
I heard—that is, I have listened to—the hair-raising (*lomaharṣaṇa*) dialogue, which causes the hair to stand on end.
The rest is clear. (74)

Viśvanātha: Beyond this, the commentary on the five verses—which constitute the final portion where the concluding verses containing the essential purport of the entire Gītā are located—has not been written again;
for Vināyaka has recently carried off those two folios by means of his own vehicle. Therefore, I have left that section out.
It was a mere repetition of what had already been said.
May He be gracious; salutations unto Him!
Thus ends the *Sārārthadarśinī*, the commentary on the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā*.
May this *Sārārthavarṣiṇī*, which showers the essential meaning and is beneficial to all people, bring joy to the virtuous and to the *cātaka* birds that are devotees.
May her sweetness delight me; may her sweetness shine within my heart.
Thus, in this delightful commentary that showers the essence of meaning for the hearts of devotees,
the eighteenth chapter of the Gītā has been appropriately concluded for the virtuous.
Thus ends the commentary *Sārārthavarṣiṇī* composed by Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravarti Ṭhakkura. [Verses 74–78]
Baladeva: The meaning of the scripture is concluded.
Now, resuming the connection of the narrative, Sañjaya said to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, "Thus I [saw]," and so forth.
It was wonderful (*adbhutam*), causing amazement to the mind because it is inconceivable within the worlds.
Romaharṣaṇa means that which produces horripilation on the body. //74//
By the grace of Vyāsa, I have heard this supreme secret— the Yoga— from Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, as he himself was speaking it directly. (18.75)

Śrīdhara: He expresses his confidence in hearing that [teaching] regarding himself with the words "by the grace of Vyāsa. Divine faculties such as sight and hearing were bestowed upon me by the blessed Vyāsa; therefore, by the grace of Vyāsa, I have heard this.
To the question "What is that?", he replies: "the supreme yoga."
He reveals his status as a superior by stating that he heard this directly from the Lord of Yoga, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, as He was speaking in person. //75//
Baladeva: By the words "by Vyāsa," he declares his own fitness for hearing that conversation which was separated [in time].
Through the grace of Vyāsa—consisting of the attainment of divine sight, hearing, and so forth granted by him—he heard this secret.
To the question "What is this?", he replies: "the supreme yoga."
The meaning is: *karma-yoga*, *jñāna-yoga*, and *bhakti-yoga*.
He establishes their supremacy by means of the phrase "from the Lord of Yoga" (*yogeśvara*).
*Yoga* is the inherent connection of all living beings, including gods and humans, with their own essential nature.
"I have heard [it] directly from Kṛṣṇa himself, the controller of their lords, and not through tradition"— thus he praises his own good fortune. //75//
O King, remembering again and again this wonderful and holy dialogue between Keśava and Arjuna, I rejoice over and over again. (18.76)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, "O King" means that I rejoice, my hair stands on end, or I attain great joy;
the rest is clear. //76//
Baladeva said: O King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, this meritorious account removes all defects up to the very limit of ignorance for one who hears it;
at every moment, I rejoice again and again and my hair stands on end. (76)
O King, remembering again and again that most wonderful form of Hari, my amazement is great, and I rejoice over and over again. (18.77)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, "and what that is" refers to the universal form (viśva-rūpa). The rest is clear. //77//
Baladeva: And that universal form which was taught to Arjuna. //77//
Wherever Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, is, and wherever Pārtha, the wielder of the bow, is, there will surely be prosperity, victory, wealth, and sound policy; this is my conviction. (18.78)

Śrīdhara: With the intention that you should therefore abandon all apprehension regarding the kingdom and other matters for your sons, he says, "Wherever... My conviction—that is, my certain conclusion—is as follows: wherever, on the side of those Pāṇḍavas, the Lord of Yoga, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, is present; and wherever Pārtha, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, is—there alone, it is connected, is the royal fortune (rāja-lakṣmī) certainly established.

Therefore, even now, you should take refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa along with your sons, propitiate the Pāṇḍavas, and having entrusted everything to them, protect the life of your son; this is the intended meaning.
For one endowed with devotion to the Blessed Lord, through His grace, there arises self-realization.
"Liberation from bondage shall be attained through happiness"—
this is the summary of the meaning of the Gītā.
For it is thus:
"That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable by unswerving devotion" (Gītā 8.22).
"By unswerving devotion alone, however, O Arjuna, I can be known in such a manner" (Gītā 11.54).

Since, in such passages, it is heard that devotion to the Blessed Lord is the most effective means for liberation, exclusive devotion to Him— conjoined with the intermediate operation of knowledge arising from His grace— is the cause of liberation.
Thus it is clearly understood;
and it is logical that knowledge itself is merely an intermediate function of devotion—
for those who are constantly disciplined.
To those who worship Me with love, I give that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me. (Gītā 10.10)
Having understood this, my devotee attains to my own state,
[knowing] both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
"Know that both are indeed beginningless. (Gītā 13.19) Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that knowledge alone is devotion, for [the Lord] says:
"Being equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion unto Me. (Gītā 18.54)
Through devotion he comes to know Me in truth, both who I am and what I am.
Because of such passages as [Gītā 18.55], which speak of the perception of difference;

and when this is so, one should not suspect a contradiction with the Vedic scripture stating, "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey. This is because knowledge is a subordinate operation (*avāntara-vyāpāra*) of devotion.
For when it is said, "He cooks with wood," it does not mean that flames are incapable of performing the action. Furthermore:
For one who has supreme devotion for the Divine,
and for the teacher as for the Divine,
these meanings indeed have been explained.
The great-souled ones shine forth.
At the end of the body, the Divine reveals the supreme Brahman, the Savior.
In this case, scriptural, traditional, and Puranic statements such as "He is attained by whomsoever He chooses" become consistent.
Therefore, it is established that devotion to the Blessed Lord alone is the cause of liberation.
With that very understanding granted by him, this commentary on his *Gītā* has been composed;
may Mādhava, who is supreme bliss itself, be pleased by it.
Now, this *Gītā-subodhinī* has been composed by the ascetic Śrīdhara Svāmī, who bears the glory of the dust from the lotus feet of Paramānanda.

Having enticed himself by the power of his own audacity, does one who seeks the truth contained within the Bhagavad-gītā approach it without the nectar-like glance of the Guru’s mercy? Is he not like one who, casting away water with his own hands, desires to obtain the jewels within the ocean?
Does not a person sink in the whirlpools without a skilled helmsman?
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Supreme Truth," in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā* composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Svāmī. //78//
Baladeva: This being so, [the Lord] says "where" in order to instruct one to abandon the desire for the victory of one's own sons and the like.

"Where" means where Kṛṣṇa, the son of Vasudeva—the Lord of Yoga previously explained, whose own will governs the nature, maintenance, and activity of all other living beings—remains as a helper, even to the extent of acting as a charioteer.
Where Pārtha— the son of your father’s sister, an incarnation of Nara, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa alone, a wielder of the bow with the unbreakable Gāṇḍīva in his hand— resides;
in that very side of Yudhiṣṭhira presided over by Śrī-Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, there shall be royal fortune, victory, the cause of the defeat of enemies, supreme excellence,
and prosperity consisting of the ever-increasing expansion of royal majesty.

The term "nītiḥ" (policy) refers to the constant and stable application of justice; this is to be connected with everything that follows. As for the doubt that this scripture is primarily concerned with warfare—that is not so—because of such passages as, "Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me," and so forth.

And because of the instruction "having renounced all dharmas," it is quite correct that the duties of the four castes and the four stages of life have been described here as being for the purpose of purifying the heart and for the sake of maintaining the world. //78//
Among those many means, devotion preceded by service (*dāsya*) is considered in the *Aṣṭādaśa* [Purāṇa] to be the one that most swiftly brings about grace from Viṣṇu.
That by whom the breast-milk of Yaśodā was drunk, who was led to the charioteership of Pārtha,
and who is expanded by a multitude of excellent qualities— that supreme reality is here sung.
Having obtained this boat of desire in the ocean of the Gītā, I have plunged in, having grasped the jewels of most wonderful meanings;
yet, due to the intensity of my joy, I am not able to emerge.
That curious son of Nanda is dear to me, O father.
This commentary, titled *Śrīmad-Gītā-Bhūṣaṇa*,
has been diligently composed by Vidyābhūṣaṇa for those who long for the sweetness of love for Śrī Govinda.
O virtuous ones, moist with compassion, purify [me].
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā Upaniṣad.

**Chapter 18: Mokṣa-saṃnyāsa-yoga (The Yoga of Liberation through Renunciation)** Śrī Bhagavān said: I shall again declare that supreme knowledge, the best of all knowledge, by knowing which all sages have attained the highest perfection from this world. In this world, among all types of knowledge, the knowledge of the *Sāṅkhya* is considered the best; and among all types of duties, the duty of *yoga* is considered the best. Those who do not perceive the same thing in all beings, whether they be ignorant or learned, being deluded by the egoism of their own nature, do not attain Me, O son of Kuntī. Even the meritorious person who acts with attachment to the fruits of action attains only the worlds of the virtuous, which are subject to return. But those who perform action for the sake of sacrifice, abandoning attachment, purify even the mind of sin with the fire of wisdom. The sacrifice offered according to scriptural injunctions by those who are free from desire is called *Brahma-yajña*; it leads to the eternal Brahman. Other actions performed with desire for fruit bind one to the world of rebirth. O best of the Bharatas, know that all actions—whether mental, vocal, or physical—are born of the qualities of *prakṛti*. The deluded, identifying themselves with the body, think, "I am the doer" of these actions born of the qualities. But he who is wise knows the truth of the distinction between the qualities and the functions, and does not become attached. The quality of *sattva*, being stainless and illuminating, binds one to happiness and knowledge. The quality of *rajas*, being passionate and the source of desire and attachment, binds one to action. But the quality of *tamas*, born of ignorance, deludes all embodied beings and binds them through negligence, indolence, and sleep. When the light of wisdom shines forth equally from all gates of the body, then *sattva* prevails. Greed, activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness, and longing—these arise when *rajas* is predominant. Darkness, inertia, negligence, and even delusion—these arise when *tamas* is predominant. When *sattva* prevails, one goes to the pure worlds of the knowers of the Supreme. By *rajas*, one is born among those attached to action; and by *tamas*, one is born in the wombs of the ignorant. They say that knowledge arises from *sattva*, action from *rajas*, and negligence from *tamas*, which is the cause of ignorance. Those endowed with *sattva* go on high; those endowed with *rajas* remain in the middle; and those endowed with the base *tamas* go downward, enveloped in the darkness of ignorance. When the seer perceives no other agent than the qualities, and realizes that which is beyond the qualities, he attains My state. When the embodied being transcends these three qualities, which are the sources of the body's afflictions, he is freed from birth, death, old age, and sorrow, and attains immortality. Arjuna said: By what characteristics, O Lord, is one who has transcended the qualities known? How does such a one conduct himself, and how does he transcend these three qualities? The Blessed Lord said: He who hates none, desires nothing, and remains unshaken by the qualities of nature, being established in the Self, is known as one who has transcended the qualities. He who is situated in equanimity amidst the arising and passing away of the qualities, who is self-contained and undisturbed, transcends the qualities. He who regards with equal vision a lump of earth, a stone, and gold, who finds pleasure and pain alike, and to whom praise and blame are the same, is transcendent. He who is the same toward friends and foes, and toward those who are neutral, as well as toward those who are well-wishers, enemies, and the indifferent; who remains the same in honor and dishonor; Who remains the same in heat and cold, in pleasure and pain, and is free from attachment; to whom praise and blame are equal, and who is silent and content with whatever comes; Who is homeless, steady-minded, firm in his resolve, and who has transcended the qualities, such a person is fit for union with Brahman.
